69085.q: Which Roman building in Augusta Raurica is still used for performances today?
69085.e: The Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica is the best preserved north of the Alps. Opposite it, on a hill, stood the Schönbühl temple.
69085.m: Performances take place today in the Roman theatre of Augusta Raurica.

69086.q: Which present-day town in the canton of Vaud stands on the site of Aventicum, the main town of the Helvetii?
69086.e: From the 1st to the 3rd century, Aventicum was the largest town on Swiss soil. At times around 20,000 people probably lived there.

69087.q: Which emperor made Aventicum a colony around AD 70?
69087.e: According to Suetonius, Vespasian’s father had lived among the Helvetii as a moneylender and died there. The town then bore the epithet Flavia.

69088.q: Where does the Cigognier sanctuary in Aventicum get its name from?
a: From a stork’s nest on its last standing column
From a god in the shape of a stork
From the storks on a mosaic
69088.e: The only surviving column is about 12 metres high. ‘Cigogne’ is the French word for stork.
69088.m: The Cigognier is named after a stork’s nest.

69089.q: Which find was discovered in 1939 in a drain near the Cigognier sanctuary?
a: A gold bust of Emperor Marcus Aurelius
69089.e: The bust is 33.5 cm high and weighs about 1.6 kg. It was probably hidden from plundering Alemanni.
69089.m: A gold bust of Marcus Aurelius was found in Aventicum in 1939.

69090.q: What happened to the Grange des Dîmes temple in Aventicum in the early Middle Ages?
a: It was turned into a church
It was extended into a castle
It was used as a grain mill
It was taken to Rome stone by stone
69090.e: The podium temple had been built in the early 2nd century on an older Celtic place of worship. Later, Christians continued to use the site.
69090.m: The Grange des Dîmes temple became a church.

69091.q: Roughly how many spectators did the amphitheatre of Aventicum hold?
69091.e: Animal hunts and gladiator fights took place in the amphitheatre. Today it is used for concerts and opera performances.
69091.m: The amphitheatre of Aventicum held about 15,000 people.

69092.q: Which British anthropologist coined the term ‘animism’ in 1871 as the basis of a theory of religion?
69092.e: Tylor presented his theory of animism in his main work ‘Primitive Culture’. He is regarded as one of the founders of anthropology in Britain.
69092.m: Edward Burnett Tylor made animism a key term in the anthropology of religion.

69093.q: What is Tylor’s famous ‘minimum definition’ of religion?
a: Fear of the forces of nature
69093.e: Tylor defined religion briefly as ‘belief in spiritual beings’. He wanted a definition that would fit all cultures.
69093.m: For Tylor, religion begins with belief in spiritual beings.

69094.q: From which experiences did Tylor derive the origin of the idea of the soul?
69094.e: Tylor suspected that early humans concluded from dream images and from the difference between the living and the dead that there is a soul separable from the body. They then transferred this idea to animals, plants and things.
69094.m: Tylor explained belief in souls through experiences of dreams and death.

69095.q: Which Latin root is contained in the term ‘animism’?
69095.e: The Latin word ‘anima’ means soul, breath or breeze. Animism refers to the idea that beings and things have a soul.
69095.m: The word animism contains the Latin anima, meaning soul.

69096.q: Which school of thought is Tylor’s theory of religion assigned to?
69096.e: Tylor arranged cultures on a ladder of development from ‘simple’ to ‘civilised’, with animism at the start. Today this stage model is criticised as Eurocentric.
69096.m: Tylor saw animism as an early stage of cultural development.

69097.q: Which idea does the term ‘animism’ describe?
a: Animals, plants and things have souls
The world is clockwork without spirit
69097.e: Animism is the belief that beings and things in nature have a soul or spirit. The word comes from the Latin anima, soul.
69097.m: In animism, nature and things have souls.

69098.q: In which religion do researchers find especially clear animist ideas?
a: In Japanese Shinto with its kami
69098.e: Shinto worships kami, spirit beings that can live in mountains, trees, rivers or rocks. This matches the animist idea of a nature filled with souls.
69098.m: In Shinto, kami live in nature and in things.

69099.q: In which work of 1912 did Émile Durkheim develop his theory of totemism?
a: The Elementary Forms of Religious Life
The Division of Labour in Society
69099.e: In ‘Les formes élémentaires de la vie religieuse’, Durkheim studied religion using reports about Australian clans. The other titles are earlier works by Durkheim on other subjects.
69099.m: Durkheim’s sociology of religion is in ‘The Elementary Forms of Religious Life’.

69100.q: Which distinction does Durkheim put at the centre of his definition of religion?
69100.e: For Durkheim, all religions divide the world into the realm of the sacred and that of the everyday, or profane. Sacred things are set apart and protected by prohibitions.
69100.m: Durkheim saw the separation of sacred and profane as the core of religion.

69101.q: According to Durkheim, what does the totem ultimately symbolise?
a: The spirit of a single ancestor
69101.e: Durkheim interpreted the totem as the emblem of the group: whoever worships the totem is really worshipping their own community. Religion thus strengthens social cohesion.
69101.m: According to Durkheim, a group worships itself in the totem.

69102.q: According to Durkheim, what do people experience at large shared ritual festivals?
69102.e: Durkheim called this excitement collective effervescence. He saw it as the origin of the experience of the sacred.
69102.m: According to Durkheim, shared rituals create overwhelming excitement.

69104.q: What did Durkheim call the moral community bound together by a religion?
69104.e: Durkheim defined religion as a system of beliefs and practices that unites all its followers in a moral community called a church. In this way he distinguished religion from private magic.
69104.m: Durkheim called the religious community, in a broad sense, a church.

69105.q: Which anthropologist criticised totemism in 1962 as an artificial research category?
69105.e: In ‘Le totémisme aujourd’hui’, Lévi-Strauss argued that animals served not as objects of worship but as tools for thinking, to distinguish social groups. Animals were ‘good to think with’.
69105.m: Lévi-Strauss saw totem animals as a means of ordering society.

69106.q: Which region of the world does the religious term ‘mana’ come from?
69106.e: The word comes from the languages of the Pacific islands. European researchers took it into religious studies in the 19th century.
69106.m: The term mana comes from the Pacific region.

69107.q: What does ‘mana’ refer to in the anthropology of religion?
69107.e: Mana is regarded as a power that makes people successful and mighty and can show itself in persons, objects or places. It is not tied to a particular being.
69107.m: Mana is an impersonal power that gives success and might.

69108.q: According to traditional belief, who has especially much mana in Polynesian societies?
69108.e: Mana shows itself in success, power and prestige. That is why chiefs were regarded as bearers of especially much mana.
69108.m: Chiefs were regarded as bearers of much mana.

69109.q: Which Polynesian term for a sacred prohibition is closely linked to mana and is also used in English today?
69109.e: Whatever has much mana often may not be touched and is ‘taboo’. The word reached Europe through James Cook.
69109.m: The word taboo comes from Polynesia.

69110.q: Which language region does the word ‘taboo’ come from?
69110.e: The Tongan word ‘tapu’ refers to something sacred or forbidden. Related forms exist in many Polynesian languages.
69110.m: The word taboo comes from Polynesian Tonga.

69111.q: Which seafarer brought the word ‘taboo’ to Europe after his visit to Tonga?
69111.e: Cook noted the word as ‘taboo’ during his visit to Tonga in 1777. Through his travel account it then spread into the European languages.
69111.m: James Cook made the word taboo known in Europe.

69113.q: What characterises a taboo in the original Polynesian sense?
a: It is both sacred and dangerous
It is a state criminal law
69113.e: A taboo protects something charged with supernatural power. According to this idea, whoever breaks it is in danger themselves, even without human punishment.
69113.m: A taboo protects something sacred that is also regarded as dangerous.

69114.q: What is Mircea Eliade’s central definition of shamanism?
69114.e: Eliade called his 1951 book ‘Shamanism: Archaic Techniques of Ecstasy’. At its centre is the shaman’s controlled ecstasy.
69114.m: For Eliade, shamanism is above all a technique of ecstasy.

69115.q: Which region does the word ‘shaman’ originally come from?
69115.e: The word comes from the language of the Evenks, a people in Siberia. Through Russian reports it reached Europe, and today it is used for similar figures worldwide.
69115.m: The word shaman comes from Siberia.

69116.q: According to Eliade, what does the shaman undertake during ecstasy?
a: A soul journey to other worlds
69116.e: According to Eliade, the shaman’s soul leaves the body and travels to the upper or lower world. There it negotiates with spirits, for example, or searches for the soul of a sick person.
69116.m: In ecstasy, the shaman undertakes a soul journey.

69117.q: Which image does Eliade use for the link between the levels of the world that the shaman passes through?
a: The world axis or world tree
69117.e: Eliade spoke of the ‘axis mundi’, which connects the underworld, earth and sky. It is often shown as a tree, pole or mountain up which the shaman climbs.
69117.m: In many shamanic ideas, the world axis connects the levels of the world.

69118.q: Which experience does Eliade describe as typical of the calling of future shamans?
a: A crisis with visions of being torn apart and renewed
Inheriting the office without any test
Buying the office from the predecessor
69118.e: Many accounts describe an initiation illness in which those called dream of being taken apart by spirits and put back together. Afterwards they are regarded as transformed.
69118.m: The shamanic calling often begins with a crisis of death and rebirth.

69119.q: What is the drum of Siberian shamans often compared to?
a: A mount for the soul journey
69119.e: In many Siberian traditions, the drum is regarded as a horse or reindeer on which the shaman rides into the spirit world. Its rhythm helps the trance.
69119.m: The shaman’s drum is often regarded as the soul’s mount.

a: Shamanic practices offered in courses in the West
The training of doctors in Asia
69120.e: Since the 1980s, courses in the West have offered simplified shamanic techniques. Critics accuse such offerings of taking traditions out of their context.
69120.m: Neoshamanism brings shamanic practices to the West.

69121.q: Which Confucian virtue is one foundation of Chinese ancestor veneration?
69121.e: Xiao demands respect and care for parents and ancestors, even beyond death. Offerings to the ancestors are seen as an expression of this duty.
69121.m: In China, filial piety obliges people to honour their ancestors.

69122.q: At which Chinese festival are the graves of the ancestors traditionally cleaned?
69122.e: At the Qingming Festival in spring, families visit the graves, clean them and bring offerings. It is a public holiday in China.
69122.m: At the Qingming Festival, Chinese families tend their ancestors’ graves.

69123.q: At which Japanese festival do the spirits of the ancestors return to their families, according to tradition?
69123.e: During Obon in summer, lanterns are lit to guide the ancestors home and then back again. The Bon dance is part of this festival.
69123.m: At the Obon festival in Japan, the returning ancestors are honoured.

69124.q: What stands in many Japanese homes to honour the deceased ancestors?
69124.e: The butsudan holds memorial tablets of the ancestors, before which incense and food are offered. A torii, by contrast, is the gate of a Shinto shrine.
69124.m: The butsudan is the Japanese household altar for the ancestors.

69125.q: What happens during the famadihana in Madagascar?
a: The ancestors’ remains are wrapped anew
The ancestors are burnt at sea
A cow is sacrificed for the king
Children are given an ancestor’s name
69125.e: At the famadihana, families open the tomb, wrap the dead in new silk cloths and dance with them. The festival strengthens the bond between the living and the ancestors.
69125.m: At the famadihana in Madagascar, the dead are wrapped anew.

69126.q: What is meant by ancestor worship?
a: The worship of a single creator god
69126.e: In ancestor worship, families honour their dead forebears, for example with gifts, prayers or festivals. It is often believed that the ancestors can protect the living.
69126.m: Ancestor worship is the veneration of dead forebears.

69127.q: At which Korean harvest festival do many families hold ancestral rites with food offerings?
69127.e: At Chuseok in autumn, many Koreans travel to their home towns and prepare a table of food for the ancestors. Afterwards they often visit the graves.
69127.m: At the Chuseok festival, Korean families honour their ancestors.

69128.q: In which country and region is Candomblé especially widespread?
69128.e: Candomblé arose in the 19th century among enslaved Africans in Brazil. Salvador da Bahia is regarded as its centre.
69128.m: Candomblé is an Afro-Brazilian religion centred in Bahia.

69129.q: What are the deities worshipped in Candomblé called?
69129.e: The orixás come from the religion of the Yoruba and embody forces of nature and areas of life.
69129.m: In Candomblé the orixás are worshipped.

69130.q: Where do the religious roots of Candomblé lie?
69130.e: Enslaved people from West Africa, such as the Yoruba and Fon, brought their religions to Brazil. Ceremonies take place in places of worship called terreiros.

69131.q: Which title refers to the leading priestess of a Candomblé house?
69131.e: The mãe de santo, also called ialorixá, leads the community and initiates new members. Her male counterpart is called pai de santo.
69131.m: The mãe de santo leads a Candomblé house.

69132.q: In honour of which orixá do thousands go to the sea with flowers in Salvador on 2 February?
69132.e: Iemanjá is regarded as the mother of the waters and queen of the sea. On 2 February, believers in the Rio Vermelho district bring gifts that are taken out to sea.
69132.m: In Salvador, Iemanjá is celebrated on 2 February as mistress of the sea.

69133.q: Why were African deities linked with Catholic saints in Candomblé?
a: So that enslaved people could secretly keep up their faith
The deities originally came from Rome
The saints were all born in Africa
69133.e: The orixás were hidden behind Catholic saints, for example Oxalá behind the Senhor do Bonfim. This blending of religions is called syncretism.
69133.m: In Candomblé, orixás are hidden behind Catholic saints.

69134.q: What role do drums and dance play in Candomblé ceremonies?
a: They call the orixás, who appear in trance
They are only there to entertain the guests
69134.e: To certain rhythms and songs, the orixás are said to enter initiated believers. These then dance in trance as embodiments of the deity.
69134.m: In Candomblé, drums call the orixás.

69135.q: On which island did the Afro-American religion Santería arise?
69135.e: Santería arose in Cuba among enslaved people from West Africa. Haiti, by contrast, is the home of Vodou, and Jamaica that of the Rastafari.

69136.q: From which two traditions did Santería mainly arise?
a: The religion of the Yoruba and Catholicism
The religion of the Maya and Protestantism
69136.e: Enslaved Yoruba from West Africa brought their religion to Cuba. There it combined with the Catholicism of the Spanish colonial rulers.
69136.m: Santería combines Yoruba religion and Catholicism.

69137.q: Why did enslaved Africans in Cuba link their deities with Catholic saints?
a: So they could keep worshipping their deities in secret
Because their deities came from Spain
Because they wanted to convert to Islam
Because the saints had originated in Africa
69137.e: The colonial rulers demanded the Catholic faith. By seeing their orishas behind images of saints, the enslaved people could preserve their own religion.
69137.m: In Cuba, believers worshipped their orishas behind Catholic saints.

69138.q: What are the deities of Santería called, which come from the religion of the Yoruba?
69138.e: Orishas are divine beings who rule over areas such as thunder, the sea or love. Kami are deities of Shinto, devas gods in Hinduism, lwa spirit beings in Vodou.
69138.m: The deities of Santería are called orishas.

69139.q: What is typical of Santería ceremonies?
a: Drumming, singing and dancing for the orishas
Sitting in silence with no music at all
A month of fasting like Ramadan
69139.e: At festivals, the orishas are called with sacred drums, songs and dances. The music has African roots and also shapes Cuban folk music.
69139.m: Drums and dance are part of Santería ceremonies.

69140.q: How did the US Supreme Court rule in 1993 in the case ‘Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye v. City of Hialeah’?
a: The targeted ban on animal sacrifice violated religious freedom
The church lost its status as a religion
The city was allowed to close the church
69140.e: The city of Hialeah in Florida had passed ordinances that specifically targeted Santería animal sacrifices. The court unanimously declared them unconstitutional.
69140.m: In 1993 the Supreme Court protected Santería rituals from targeted bans.

69141.q: What do newly initiated members of Santería, the iyawó, wear for a year?
69141.e: After the initiation, the ‘asiento’, the person is regarded as newborn and dresses entirely in white for a year. Further rules of behaviour go with this.
69141.m: Newly initiated members of Santería wear white for a year.

69142.q: What does syncretism mean in religious studies?
a: The blending of elements from different religions
The splitting of a religion into two churches
The banning of a religion by the state
The literal interpretation of holy scriptures
69142.e: Syncretism often arises when cultures meet. Examples are Santería in Cuba or the equating of Greek and Roman gods.
69142.m: Syncretism is the blending of religions.

69143.q: What is the Roman practice of equating foreign gods with their own deities called?
69143.e: In this way the Romans interpreted Germanic or Celtic gods as Mercury or Mars, for example. The expression goes back to Tacitus.
69143.m: The interpretatio Romana equated foreign gods with Roman ones.

69144.q: Which Brazilian religion arose at the start of the 20th century from Afro-Brazilian traditions, Catholicism and the spiritism of Allan Kardec?
69144.e: Umbanda is said to have arisen in Rio de Janeiro in 1908. It combines orixás and spirits of ancestors with Catholic saints and spiritist teachings.
69144.m: Umbanda is a syncretic religion from Brazil.

69145.q: Which Vietnamese religion venerates the French writer Victor Hugo among its saints?
69145.e: Caodaism, founded in 1926, combines elements of Buddhism, Daoism, Confucianism and Christianity. There, Victor Hugo is regarded as a spirit being who passes on messages.
69145.m: Caodaism is a syncretic religion from Vietnam.

69146.q: Why is the veneration of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico often seen as an example of syncretism?
a: A shrine to an Aztec goddess used to stand on the site
Mary appeared there to a Spanish king
The church was built by Muslims
Only Maya gods are worshipped there
69146.e: The apparition of 1531 is said to have taken place on Tepeyac hill, where the mother goddess Tonantzin had been worshipped before. In this way old and new faith combined.
69146.m: Guadalupe combines devotion to Mary with Aztec roots.

69147.q: What did theologians in the 17th century accuse someone of when they called him a ‘syncretist’?
a: Mixing the teachings of different denominations
Believing in no god at all
69147.e: In the syncretistic controversy, the Lutheran Georg Calixtus was attacked because he sought an understanding between the denominations. His opponents saw this as improper mixing.
69147.m: In the 17th century, ‘syncretist’ was an accusation of mixing doctrines.

69148.q: What are the spirit beings in Haitian Vodou called, which are often equated with Catholic saints?
69148.e: The lwa (also loa) are spirit beings who mediate between people and the distant creator god. In Vodou they are often shown with images of Catholic saints.
69148.m: In Haitian Vodou the spirit beings are called lwa.

69149.q: Which figure do many people in the Andes worship as ‘Mother Earth’?
69149.e: Pachamama is regarded as the nourishing but also demanding earth, to whom people give back gifts before work and festivals. Mama Quilla, by contrast, is the moon goddess of the Inca.
69149.m: Pachamama is the Mother Earth worshipped in the Andes.

69150.q: What do many people in the Andes worship as apus?
a: The mummies of the Inca kings
The stars of the Milky Way
69150.e: Apus are the spirits of great mountains that watch over water, herds and health. People ask them for protection in rituals.
69150.m: In the Andes, the apus are the spirits of the mountains.

69151.q: What do people in the Andes give back to Pachamama in rituals?
a: Gifts such as coca leaves, seeds and sweets
69151.e: Such gifts are often bundled into a package, a despacho, and then burnt or buried. In this way people thank the earth and the mountains.
69151.m: In the Andes, people give gifts back to Pachamama.

69152.q: Which month is regarded in many Andean areas as the special month of Pachamama?
69152.e: In August, before sowing, the earth is regarded as ‘open’ and hungry. That is why especially many gifts are offered to her at the start of the month.
69152.m: In the Andes, August is the month of Pachamama.

69153.q: Which plant is an especially important gift to the earth and mountains in Andean rituals?
69153.e: In the k’intu, three fine coca leaves are held like a fan, breathed upon and dedicated to the sacred powers. Coca has been regarded as a sacred plant in the Andes for centuries.
69153.m: Coca leaves are an important gift in Andean rituals.

69154.q: What does the Qoyllur Rit’i pilgrimage in Peru combine?
a: Christianity and the veneration of sacred mountains
69154.e: The pilgrimage to the glacier on Mount Ausangate combines Catholic devotion to Christ with honouring sacred mountains. It has been UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage since 2011.
69154.m: The Qoyllur Rit’i pilgrimage combines Christianity and mountain veneration.

69155.q: What do people buy at the Alasitas fair in La Paz so that their wishes come true?
a: Miniatures of houses, cars or banknotes
69155.e: The miniatures are blessed and dedicated to the Ekeko, the figure of prosperity and abundance. In this way the wishes are meant to come true in the coming year.
69155.m: At the Alasitas fair, people buy miniatures for their wishes.

69156.q: Which plant is used as a sacrament in the Native American Church?
69156.e: The peyote cactus is eaten or drunk as tea during the service and is regarded as sacred medicine. Its use is protected by law for members in the USA.
69156.m: The Native American Church uses peyote as a sacrament.

69157.q: Who mainly belongs to the Native American Church?
a: Members of the Indigenous peoples of North America
69157.e: The Native American Church is the largest religious community of Indigenous peoples in the USA. It was officially founded in 1918.
69157.m: The Native American Church is a church of the Indigenous peoples of North America.

69158.q: When does a traditional ceremony of the Native American Church take place?
a: For an hour every Sunday morning
69158.e: The participants sit around the fire all night, praying, singing and drumming. A leader, the roadman, guides them through the ceremony.
69158.m: The peyote ceremony lasts all night.

69159.q: In which kind of dwelling does the classic ceremony of the Native American Church take place?
69159.e: An earth altar is built in the tipi, and a fire burns in front of it all night. The tipi is the traditional tent of the Plains peoples.
69159.m: The ceremony takes place in a tipi.

69160.q: Which religion does the Native American Church combine with Indigenous traditions?
69160.e: In the ceremonies people often pray to God and Jesus, while peyote is regarded as sacred medicine. In this way Christian and Indigenous elements combine.
69160.m: The Native American Church combines Christianity and Indigenous traditions.

69161.q: Which psychoactive substance is contained in the peyote cactus?
69161.e: Mescaline is an alkaloid that causes strong changes in perception. Outside protected religious use, mescaline is banned in many countries, including Switzerland.

69162.q: Why are members of the Native American Church in the USA allowed to use peyote?
a: Religious use is protected by law
The church has its own police force
69162.e: Since 1994 a federal law has protected the religious use of peyote by Native Americans. Outside this use, mescaline is banned.
69162.m: Since 1994 a federal law has protected religious peyote use.

69163.q: What do the songlines of the Aboriginal peoples describe?
a: Paths of the creator ancestors across the land
69163.e: Songlines follow the paths on which ancestral beings shaped the land in the time of creation. Whoever knows the songs can find waterholes and landmarks in the right order.
69163.m: Songlines connect songs, creation stories and landscape.

69164.q: How are songlines passed on from generation to generation?
a: Orally, through songs, dances and stories
69164.e: The Aboriginal peoples had no writing. Elders pass on the songs and knowledge of routes, waterholes and laws to younger people.

69165.q: What significance does the land have in Aboriginal religion?
a: It is sacred and connected with the stories of the ancestors
It is just grazing land with no religious meaning
It belongs only to the gods in the sky
It is regarded as unclean and dangerous
69165.e: For Aboriginal peoples, ancestral beings shaped the land and are present in it. Mountains, rocks and waterholes tell their stories.
69165.m: For Aboriginal peoples, the land is sacred.

69166.q: Since when has climbing Uluru been banned?
69166.e: For decades, the traditional owners had asked visitors not to climb the sacred rock. Since 26 October 2019, the climb has been banned completely.
69166.m: Uluru may no longer be climbed since October 2019.

69167.q: Which group of stars is at the centre of the ‘Seven Sisters’ songline?
69167.e: The songline tells how seven sisters flee across the continent from a pursuer and finally become stars. The National Museum of Australia devoted a major exhibition to it in 2017.
69167.m: The Aboriginal Seven Sisters are the Pleiades.

69168.q: With which English term did anthropologists around 1900 translate the Arrernte word ‘Alcheringa’?
69168.e: Baldwin Spencer and Francis Gillen rendered the word as ‘dream times’. Many Aboriginal people find the term inaccurate, as it is not about dreams but about an ever-present order of creation.
69168.m: The translation Dreamtime goes back to Spencer and Gillen.

69169.q: What function did songlines serve for travelling across the land?
a: They served as a sung map
They served as a calendar for the harvest
They served as a tax list
They served as a register of ancestors
69169.e: The verses name landmarks in the order in which you come across them. In this way people could find routes and waterholes even over long distances.
69169.m: Songlines could be used like a sung map.

69170.q: Who is regarded as the founder of the modern Wicca religion?
69170.e: Gerald Gardner made Wicca publicly known in England in the 1950s. Alex Sanders and Raymond Buckland later founded their own branches or spread Wicca in the USA.
69170.m: Gerald Gardner is regarded as the founder of Wicca.

69171.q: How did Gerald Gardner present Wicca in his 1954 book?
a: As a surviving ancient witch religion
69171.e: Gardner claimed that Wicca was an ancient witch religion that had survived in secret. Historians today see Wicca as a new religion of the 20th century.
69171.m: Gardner presented Wicca as an ancient witch religion.

69172.q: What is the core of the ‘Wiccan Rede’?
a: If it harms no one, do what you will
As you sow, so shall you reap
Honour the gods and fear them
69172.e: The Rede reads ‘An it harm none, do what ye will’. It is regarded as the most important ethical principle of many Wicca groups.
69172.m: The Wiccan Rede demands harming no one.

69173.q: How many festivals of the year, so-called sabbats, does Wicca celebrate?
69173.e: The Wheel of the Year includes the four solstices and equinoxes and four festivals in between, such as Samhain and Beltane. This makes a wheel of eight festivals.
69173.m: Wicca celebrates eight festivals in the Wheel of the Year.

69174.q: Which deities are at the centre for many Wicca groups?
a: A goddess and a horned god
The ancestors of the imperial house
69174.e: Many Wicca groups worship a moon goddess and a horned god as a pair. They stand for the female and male forces of nature.
69174.m: Wicca often worships a goddess and a horned god.

69175.q: Which neopagan religion arose in England in the middle of the 20th century?
69175.e: Wicca became known from the 1950s through Gerald Gardner. The movement claims to continue a supposedly ancient witch religion.
69175.m: Wicca arose in England in the 20th century.

69176.q: Which place in England do modern druids visit especially at the summer solstice?
69176.e: Every year thousands celebrate sunrise on the longest day at the stone circle of Stonehenge. Modern druids hold ceremonies there.
69176.m: Modern druids celebrate the solstice at Stonehenge.

69177.q: Which gods does the Icelandic Ásatrú movement draw on?
a: The Norse gods such as Odin and Thor
The Greek gods such as Zeus
The Egyptian gods such as Ra
The Roman gods such as Jupiter
69177.e: Ásatrú means ‘faith in the Aesir’, the Norse gods. In Iceland the community has been officially recognised since 1973.

69178.q: In which country was an Ásatrú community founded in 1972 and officially recognised just a year later?
69178.e: The community Ásatrúarfélagið formed in 1972 around the poet Sveinbjörn Beinteinsson. In 1973 it received official recognition as a religious community.
69178.m: Ásatrú is officially recognised in Iceland.

69179.q: What does the name ‘Ásatrú’ roughly mean?
69179.e: The Aesir are one of the two groups of gods in Norse mythology, which includes Odin and Thor, for example. ‘Trú’ means faith or loyalty.
69179.m: Ásatrú means faith in the Aesir.

69180.q: What is the central sacrificial and festive ritual in Ásatrú called?
69180.e: At a blót, food and drink are offered to the gods, usually mead or beer. The term comes from Old Norse.
69180.m: The blót is the most important ritual in Ásatrú.

69181.q: What happens at a sumbel, a ritual in Ásatrú?
a: A drinking horn is passed round and gods and ancestors are honoured
People stay silent for a whole day
Weapons are sunk in a bog
People read from the Bible together
69181.e: At a sumbel, a horn goes round in several rounds, and the participants honour gods and ancestors or make vows. Seiðr and galdr, by contrast, refer to forms of magic.
69181.m: At a sumbel, toasts are made in rounds.

69182.q: Which medieval collections of texts are important sources for Ásatrú?
a: The Poetic Edda and the Prose Edda
The Kalevala and the Beowulf saga
69182.e: The Eddas were written down in Iceland in the 13th century and contain myths about the Norse gods. They are the main source for today’s reconstruction.
69182.m: The two Eddas are the main sources for Ásatrú.

69183.q: Which day of the week is named after the Norse god Thor, who is worshipped in Ásatrú?
69183.e: Thursday is the day of the thunder god, called Donar in the south and Thor in the north. Friday, by contrast, goes back to a goddess.
69183.m: Thursday is named after the thunder god Thor.

69184.q: Which second group of gods besides the Aesir does Norse mythology know?
69184.e: The Vanir include Njord, Freyr and Freyja, for example. According to myth, the Aesir and Vanir went to war and then made peace.
69184.m: Besides the Aesir, Norse mythology has the Vanir.

69185.q: In which region of the world did most cargo cults arise?
69185.e: Cargo cults arose mainly in New Guinea and on islands such as Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands. They were reactions to colonial encounters with the goods and power of foreigners.
69185.m: Cargo cults arose mainly in Melanesia.

69186.q: Who is John Frum for the followers of the John Frum movement in Vanuatu?
a: A spirit being who is meant to bring wealth and goods
69186.e: The movement arose in the late 1930s on the island of Tanna. Its followers expect John Frum to bring goods and wealth.
69186.m: John Frum is meant to bring his followers wealth.

69187.q: Which country plays a special role in the John Frum movement?
69187.e: In the Second World War, American troops came to Vanuatu with lots of goods. On John Frum Day, men still march with bamboo rifles and ‘USA’ on their chests.
69187.m: The John Frum movement reveres the USA as the source of the goods.

69188.q: What did followers of some cargo cults build copies of to attract cargo?
69188.e: The followers imitated what they had seen among foreigners: airstrips, wooden radios or drill exercises. They hoped that this would bring the goods of the ancestors to them.
69188.m: Cargo cults imitated airstrips to attract goods.

69189.q: Which person was worshipped as a divine being in villages on Tanna?
69189.e: People in some villages saw Prince Philip as the son of a mountain spirit who had gone across the sea. After his death in 2021 they held mourning ceremonies.
69189.m: On Tanna, Prince Philip was worshipped as a divine being.

69190.q: In which period did many cargo cults spread especially strongly?
a: During and after the Second World War
69190.e: In the Second World War, troops brought huge quantities of goods to the islands of Melanesia. Early cults such as the Vailala Madness of 1919 existed before that, though.
69190.m: Many cargo cults flourished during and after the Second World War.

69191.q: Which physicist coined the term ‘cargo cult science’ in a speech in 1974?
69191.e: At Caltech, Feynman criticised research that looks scientific on the outside but lacks the core of honest testing. He compared it to rituals that imitate outward forms without the hoped-for result happening.
69191.m: Richard Feynman spoke of cargo cult science in 1974.

69192.q: In which era did the Greek philosopher Epicurus live?
a: In the Hellenistic period, after Alexander the Great
69192.e: Epicurus lived from 341 to 270 BC. This means he worked after Socrates, Plato and Aristotle, in the Hellenistic period.
69192.m: Epicurus was one of the philosophers of the Hellenistic period.

69193.q: What was the school that Epicurus founded in Athens around 306 BC called?
69193.e: Epicurus bought a property with a garden in Athens, where he lived and taught with his students. His school was therefore called ‘Kepos’, ‘The Garden’.
69193.m: Epicurus’s school was called ‘The Garden’ after its location.

69194.q: Which state of the soul did Epicurus strive for as the goal of a happy life?
69194.e: For Epicurus, happiness lay in the absence of bodily pain and mental unrest. He called this peace of mind ataraxia.
69194.m: Epicurus sought happiness in peace of mind.

69195.q: What idea did Epicurus have of the gods?
a: They exist but do not care about humans
They do not exist and are pure invention
They steer every single human fate
They demand daily animal sacrifices in thanks
69195.e: Epicurus did not deny the gods, but thought they lived in bliss in the spaces between worlds and did not interfere in events. So there was no need to fear them.
69195.m: According to Epicurus, no one need fear the gods, because they do not interfere.

69196.q: From which earlier philosopher did Epicurus take the teaching that everything is made of atoms?
69196.e: Epicurus built his natural philosophy on the atomism of Democritus. He explained the world from atoms and empty space, without divine intervention.
69196.m: Epicurus explained nature with atoms and empty space.

69197.q: What attitude to death did Epicurus take in his ‘Letter to Menoeceus’?
a: Death is a punishment from the gods
Death leads to a judgement of the dead
Death is the beginning of rebirth
69197.e: When we exist, death is not there, and when death is there, we no longer exist, Epicurus argued. The fear of death is therefore unfounded.
69197.m: Epicurus wanted to free people from the fear of death.

69198.q: Which philosophical problem is linked with Epicurus through the Church Father Lactantius?
69198.e: Lactantius records an argument attributed to Epicurus: how can there be evil if God is good and all-powerful? Today this question is called the problem of theodicy.
69198.m: The question of God and evil in the world is called the problem of theodicy.

69199.q: In which city did Baruch de Spinoza live when he was expelled from the Jewish community in 1656?
69199.e: Spinoza was born in Amsterdam in 1632 and placed under a ban (cherem) by the Portuguese Jewish community in 1656. The reason was his views, which were considered heretical.
69199.m: Spinoza was expelled from his community in Amsterdam in 1656.

69200.q: With which formula did Spinoza sum up his equating of God and the world?
69200.e: ‘Deus sive natura’ means ‘God, or nature’. For Spinoza, God is the one infinite substance, which is identical with nature.

69201.q: How is Spinoza’s main work, the ‘Ethics’, structured?
a: Following the geometric method, with propositions
As a dialogue between teacher and pupil
As a collection of short aphorisms
As a diary in the form of letters
69201.e: The ‘Ethics’ has the subtitle ‘ordine geometrico demonstrata’. As in mathematics, Spinoza derives propositions with proofs from definitions and axioms.
69201.m: Spinoza wrote his ‘Ethics’ like a geometry book.

69202.q: With which craft did Spinoza earn part of his living?
69202.e: Spinoza ground optical lenses for microscopes and telescopes. This work allowed him a modest, independent life as a philosopher.
69202.m: Spinoza lived modestly as a lens grinder.

69203.q: Which work by Spinoza appeared anonymously in 1670 and contained an early historical-critical interpretation of the Bible?
69203.e: In the ‘Tractatus theologico-politicus’, Spinoza called for freedom of thought and speech and read the Bible as a historical document. The book was quickly banned.
69203.m: Spinoza read the Bible as a historical document.

69204.q: What does the term ‘pantheism’, often used to describe Spinoza’s thought, mean?
a: God and the universe are one
There are many gods with their own tasks
God no longer intervenes after creation
69204.e: Pantheism comes from the Greek pan, all, and theos, god. The Irish freethinker John Toland first used the term in 1705.
69204.m: Pantheism means that God and the universe are one.

69205.q: How did churches and authorities usually judge Spinoza’s philosophy in the 17th and 18th centuries?
69205.e: Spinoza’s works were banned, and ‘Spinozist’ was long a term of abuse for the godless. Only the pantheism controversy of 1785 made him newly known in Germany.
69205.m: Spinoza was long regarded as a dangerous denier of God.

69206.q: Which physicist answered a question about his faith in 1929 by saying he believed in ‘Spinoza’s God’?
69206.e: Einstein wrote to a New York rabbi that he believed in Spinoza’s God, who reveals himself in the harmony of all that exists. He did not believe in a God who concerns himself with people’s fates.
69206.m: Einstein referred to the God of Spinoza.

69207.q: What is the core of deism?
a: God created the world but no longer intervenes
God and nature are one and the same
God constantly reveals himself through miracles
There are many gods of equal standing
69207.e: Deists believe in a creator God who can be known through reason. They reject revelation, miracles and interventions in the course of the world.
69207.m: Deism has a creator God who no longer intervenes.

69208.q: Which image is the God of deism often compared to?
69208.e: God is said to have built and wound up the world like clockwork, which then runs by itself according to fixed laws of nature. This image suited the mechanical world view of the Enlightenment.
69208.m: In deism, the world runs like wound-up clockwork.

69209.q: In which era did deism spread especially widely?
69209.e: In the 17th and 18th centuries, thinkers looked for a religion based on reason. Herbert of Cherbury is regarded as the father of English deism.
69209.m: Deism is a movement of the Enlightenment.

69210.q: In the view of deists, how is God known?
a: Through reason and the order of nature
Through the teaching of the Church alone
Not at all, because there is no God
69210.e: Deists believed that true religion can be known through reason and is as old as creation. Matthew Tindal argued this in 1730, for example.
69210.m: In deism, God is known through reason.

69211.q: Which revolutionary wrote the deist polemic ‘The Age of Reason’ (from 1794)?
69211.e: In ‘The Age of Reason’, Thomas Paine defended belief in a God but sharply criticised churches and revealed religion. The book was controversial in the USA.
69211.m: Thomas Paine spread deism with ‘The Age of Reason’.

69212.q: What did Thomas Jefferson remove in his version of the Gospels, the so-called Jefferson Bible?
a: The teachings on love of neighbour
69212.e: Jefferson cut the miracles and the resurrection out of the Gospels. What was left was Jesus as a moral teacher, which matched deist thinking.
69212.m: The Jefferson Bible shows Jesus without miracles, as a moral teacher.

69213.q: Why did many deists publish their criticism of the Bible anonymously or not at all?
a: They had to fear punishment and being shunned by society
They did not want to earn money from sales
Books were not allowed to name an author at that time
They themselves thought their ideas were wrong
69213.e: The Hamburg scholar Reimarus wrote his criticism only in secret. It was Lessing who published it from 1774 as ‘Fragments of an Anonymous Author’.
69213.m: Deists had to fear punishment for criticising the Bible.

69214.e: Voltaire (1694 to 1778) was really called François-Marie Arouet. He used the pen name Voltaire from 1718.
69214.m: Voltaire is the pen name of François-Marie Arouet.

69215.q: With which battle cry did Voltaire fight superstition and church intolerance?
69215.e: ‘Écrasez l’infâme’ means ‘Crush the infamous thing’. By this Voltaire meant the fanaticism and intolerance of the Church of his time.
69215.m: Voltaire fought religious fanaticism with ‘Écrasez l’infâme’.

69216.q: Which legal case prompted Voltaire to write his ‘Treatise on Tolerance’ in 1763?
a: The Affair of the Diamond Necklace
69216.e: The Protestant Jean Calas was executed in Toulouse in 1762, although he was innocent. Voltaire campaigned for his rehabilitation and wrote against religious intolerance.
69216.m: The Calas affair made Voltaire a champion of tolerance.

69217.q: Where did Voltaire live for about 18 years from around 1760, near the Swiss border?
69217.e: Voltaire first lived in the house ‘Les Délices’ in Geneva and then moved to his château in Ferney, just across the border. The place is called Ferney-Voltaire today.
69217.m: Voltaire lived for a long time in Ferney near Geneva.

69218.q: Which philosophical doctrine does Voltaire mock in the novel ‘Candide’ (1759)?
a: The best of all possible worlds
69218.e: In ‘Candide’, the tutor Pangloss keeps repeating, despite every disaster, that this is the best of all possible worlds. Voltaire was aiming at Leibniz’s optimism.

69219.q: Which disaster of 1755 shook Voltaire’s trust in a benevolent world order?
69219.e: The Lisbon earthquake killed tens of thousands. Voltaire then wrote the ‘Poem on the Lisbon Disaster’ and questioned divine providence.
69219.m: The Lisbon earthquake of 1755 sparked a debate about God and suffering.

69220.q: Which saying of Voltaire’s shows that, as a deist, he held on to a God?
a: ‘If God did not exist, it would be necessary to invent him.’
‘God is dead, and we have killed him.’
‘Religion is the opium of the people.’
‘Man created God in his own image.’
69220.e: Voltaire wrote this line around 1770 in a verse epistle. He rejected the Church but considered a creator God reasonable and useful for morality.
69220.m: Voltaire was a critic of the Church but not an atheist.

69221.q: Which philosopher wrote the work ‘Religion within the Bounds of Bare Reason’?
69221.e: Kant published the work in Königsberg in 1793. In it he examined what in religion can stand up before reason.
69221.m: Kant’s work on religion appeared in 1793.

69223.q: Why did Kant come into conflict with the Prussian king Frederick William II?
a: Because of his work on religion
Because of criticism of the army
69223.e: Under Frederick William II there was strict religious censorship. Kant was reprimanded and promised not to speak publicly about religion any more.
69223.m: With his work on religion, Kant came into conflict with Prussian censorship.

69224.q: According to Kant, what is religion based on?
69224.e: For Kant, religion is morality regarded as the command of God. Morality itself does not need religion as a foundation.
69224.m: For Kant, religion is based on morality, not the other way round.

69225.q: For Kant, what is true service to God?
69225.e: Kant distinguishes true service, which consists of a moral way of life, from mere ritual. According to Kant, whoever believes they can win God’s favour with rites is mistaken.
69225.m: For Kant, true worship is a moral life.

69226.q: What did Kant think of proofs of the existence of God?
a: They are not possible with reason
They are all in the Bible
69226.e: Kant considered proofs of God impossible. Nevertheless he found it reasonable to believe in God, because morality suggests this belief.
69226.m: For Kant, God can be neither proved nor disproved.

69227.q: Which motto of the Enlightenment did Kant make famous?
a: ‘Have the courage to use your own understanding!’
‘Man is the measure of all things.’
69227.e: Kant wrote this sentence in 1784 in his essay ‘What is Enlightenment?’. Everyone should think for themselves, including in matters of faith.
69227.m: Kant demanded that people think for themselves, also on questions of religion.

69228.q: In which work did Ludwig Feuerbach develop his critique of religion in 1841?
69228.e: In ‘The Essence of Christianity’, Feuerbach interpreted religion as an expression of human qualities. The book influenced the Young Hegelians and Karl Marx.
69228.m: Feuerbach’s main work is ‘The Essence of Christianity’.

69229.q: What does Feuerbach’s projection theory say?
a: Humans transfer their own nature onto God
God projects his thoughts into the world
The Church projects power onto the state
69229.e: Feuerbach thought that humans imagine their best qualities, such as love, wisdom and goodness, as an infinite being outside themselves. They call this being God.
69229.m: According to Feuerbach, God is a mirror image of humans.

69230.q: Which philosophical group did Ludwig Feuerbach belong to?
69230.e: Feuerbach had studied under Hegel in Berlin and later turned against his idealism. Together with Bruno Bauer, David Friedrich Strauss and others he counts as a Young Hegelian.

69231.q: Which sentence sums up Feuerbach’s critique of religion?
69231.e: According to Feuerbach, whoever speaks about God is really speaking about humans. That is why the secret of theology can be resolved in the study of humankind.
69231.m: For Feuerbach, the secret of theology is anthropology.

69232.q: Which Swiss writer attended Feuerbach’s lectures on the essence of religion in Heidelberg in 1848/49?
69232.e: Gottfried Keller heard Feuerbach in Heidelberg and afterwards turned away from belief in God and immortality. Feuerbach’s thinking also shaped his novel ‘Green Henry’.
69232.m: Gottfried Keller was strongly influenced by Feuerbach.

69233.q: Which well-known saying about food comes from Ludwig Feuerbach?
a: Man is a wolf to man
Man is the measure of all things
69233.e: Feuerbach wrote the sentence in 1850 in a review of a book by the physiologist Jakob Moleschott. It expresses his materialism: even thinking depends on the body.
69233.m: The saying ‘Man is what he eats’ comes from Feuerbach.

69234.q: Which thinker criticised Feuerbach in eleven short theses in 1845?
69234.e: In the ‘Theses on Feuerbach’, Marx accused him of seeing humans only in the abstract. The eleventh thesis demands not only interpreting the world but changing it.
69234.m: Marx criticised Feuerbach in the ‘Theses on Feuerbach’.

69235.q: Instead of the ‘illusory happiness’ religion offers the people, what does Marx demand?
a: The real happiness of the people
A ban on all church services
The founding of a religion of reason
69235.e: Marx wrote in 1844 that abolishing religion as illusory happiness is the demand for the real happiness of the people. The point is to change the conditions that make religion necessary.
69235.m: Marx wanted to remove the causes of religion through better living conditions.

69236.q: How does Marx describe religion just before the opium sentence?
a: As the sigh of the oppressed creature
As a tool of priestly cunning
As a childhood illness of humanity
As a mirror of divine order
69236.e: Marx calls religion the sigh of the oppressed creature and the heart of a heartless world. For him, religion is also an expression of and protest against real misery.
69236.m: Marx saw religion as an expression of real misery.

69237.q: What did Marx mean by the image of opium?
a: Religion eases suffering without removing its causes
Religion makes people aggressive and violent
Religion is heavily taxed by the state
69237.e: In the 19th century, opium was a common painkiller. Like it, religion dulls suffering instead of changing its social causes.
69237.m: For Marx, religion dulls suffering instead of removing it.

69238.q: Which sentence by Marx stands at the start of the Introduction to the Critique of Hegel’s Philosophy of Right?
a: The criticism of religion is the premise of all criticism
History is a history of class struggles
69238.e: Marx thought that the criticism of religion in Germany was essentially complete. Now the criticism of heaven had to turn into criticism of law and politics.
69238.m: For Marx, the criticism of religion was the starting point of all criticism of society.

69239.q: Which politician wrote in ‘Socialism and Religion’ in 1905 of religion as ‘opium for the people’?
69239.e: Lenin sharpened Marx’s formula: religion was deliberately given to the workers as a drug. This interpretation shaped the anti-religious policies of the Soviet Union.
69239.m: Lenin turned Marx’s formula into a political slogan.

69240.q: Which philosopher especially influenced Karl Marx’s critique of religion, because he interpreted God as a human projection?
69240.e: Feuerbach saw God as a mirror image of human qualities. Marx took over this idea and asked which social conditions make religion necessary.
69240.m: Feuerbach shaped Marx’s critique of religion.

69241.q: Where does Marx place religion in his model of base and superstructure?
a: As part of the productive forces
As part of the means of production
69241.e: Marx counts economic relations as the base. Religion, law, politics and morality form the superstructure, which is shaped by the base.
69241.m: For Marx, religion belongs to the superstructure of society.

69242.q: In which work by Nietzsche does ‘the madman’ announce the death of God (aphorism 125)?
69242.e: Aphorism 125 is in ‘The Gay Science’ of 1882. There a man in the marketplace cries: ‘God is dead!’
69242.m: Nietzsche’s ‘God is dead’ is in ‘The Gay Science’.

69243.q: With what does Nietzsche’s ‘madman’ search for God in the bright morning?
a: With a burning candle in the temple
69243.e: The madman runs into the marketplace with a lantern in the bright morning. The image recalls the ancient philosopher Diogenes, who searched for a human being with a lantern.
69243.m: Nietzsche’s madman searches for God with a lantern.

69244.q: Whom does Nietzsche’s ‘madman’ hold responsible for the death of God?
69244.e: The madman cries: ‘We have killed him, you and I!’ What is meant is that modern culture itself has dissolved belief in God.
69244.m: In Nietzsche, humans have killed God.

69245.q: What danger did Nietzsche see as a consequence of the death of God?
69245.e: If God falls away as the ground of all values, all values threaten to become meaningless. Nietzsche called this state nihilism and called for a revaluation of all values.
69245.m: Nietzsche feared nihilism after the death of God.

69246.q: At which Swiss university was Nietzsche professor of classical philology from 1869?
69246.e: Nietzsche was appointed to Basel at the age of only 24. He taught there until 1879 and later spent many summers in Sils Maria in the Engadine.
69246.m: Nietzsche was a professor in Basel.

69247.q: Which guiding figure does Nietzsche set against the dead God in ‘Thus Spoke Zarathustra’?
69247.e: Zarathustra teaches: ‘Dead are all the gods: now we want the overman to live.’ The overman is to create new values himself.
69247.m: Nietzsche put the overman in the place of God.

69248.q: In ‘On the Genealogy of Morals’ (1887), what does Nietzsche call the morality he attributes to Christianity?
69248.e: Nietzsche thought the weak, out of resentment (ressentiment), had declared humility and pity the highest values. He called this morality slave morality.
69248.m: Nietzsche interpreted Christian morality as slave morality.

69249.q: In which work of 1927 did Sigmund Freud describe religion as an illusion?
69249.e: In ‘The Future of an Illusion’, Freud interprets religious teachings as wish fulfilments. He hopes that science will one day replace them.
69249.m: In 1927 Freud called religion an illusion.

69250.q: What does Freud mean by an illusion in connection with religion?
a: A belief that arises from a wish
A deliberate lie by the priests
69250.e: For Freud, an illusion is not necessarily false, but it is driven by a wish. Religious ideas fulfil the wish for protection and comfort.
69250.m: For Freud, religion arises from human wishes.

69251.q: To which childhood experience does Freud trace the idea of God?
a: The longing for a protecting father
69251.e: The adult feels as helpless before the world as the child once did. That is why he creates in God a powerful, protecting father.
69251.m: Freud saw God as an exaggerated image of a father.

69252.q: With which mental disorder did Freud compare religious rituals in 1907?
69252.e: In ‘Obsessive Actions and Religious Practices’, Freud called religion a universal obsessional neurosis of humanity. He saw similarities between rituals and compulsive actions.
69252.m: Freud compared religious rituals to compulsive actions.

69253.q: In which work of 1912/13 does Freud explain the origin of religion through the murder of the father in the primal horde?
a: Group Psychology and the Analysis of the Ego
Jokes and Their Relation to the Unconscious
69253.e: In ‘Totem and Taboo’, Freud suggests that sons once killed the primal father and then worshipped him out of guilt. Totemism and religion are said to have arisen from this.
69253.m: In ‘Totem and Taboo’, Freud explained religion through feelings of guilt.

69254.q: How did the Zurich pastor Oskar Pfister respond to Freud’s critique of religion in 1928?
a: Freud’s faith in science was itself an illusion
Freud was right on every point
Psychoanalysis was the work of the devil
69254.e: Pfister was a pastor and psychoanalyst and a friend of Freud. His reply was titled ‘The Illusion of a Future’.
69254.m: Oskar Pfister contradicted Freud from a Christian point of view.

69255.q: What is meant by the ‘oceanic feeling’ that Freud wrote about in 1930?
a: A feeling of boundless connection with the world
69255.e: The writer Romain Rolland saw this feeling as the source of religion. Freud traced it back to early childhood experience.
69255.m: The oceanic feeling is a feeling of oneness with the universe.

69256.q: Which four authors are known as ‘the four horsemen’ of New Atheism?
69256.e: The four met in 2007 for a filmed conversation that became known as ‘The Four Horsemen’. They are regarded as the main representatives of New Atheism.
69256.m: Dawkins, Dennett, Harris and Hitchens are the ‘four horsemen’ of New Atheism.

69257.q: Which book by Richard Dawkins appeared in 2006 and became the bestseller of New Atheism?
69257.e: ‘The God Delusion’ appeared in German in 2007 as ‘Der Gotteswahn’. In it Dawkins argues that the existence of God is very improbable.

69258.q: Which book by Sam Harris (2004) is often seen as the beginning of New Atheism?
69258.e: Sam Harris wrote ‘The End of Faith’ under the impression of the attacks of 11 September 2001. In it he criticises religious faith as a danger.
69258.m: Sam Harris launched New Atheism with ‘The End of Faith’.

69259.q: Which journalist wrote ‘God Is Not Great’ in 2007?
69259.e: Christopher Hitchens was a British-American writer. In ‘God Is Not Great’ he accuses religion of poisoning many things.
69259.m: Christopher Hitchens wrote ‘God Is Not Great’.

69260.q: How does the philosopher Daniel Dennett explain the origin of religion?
69260.e: Dennett studies religion as a natural phenomenon. He calls for it to be researched scientifically like other human behaviour.
69260.m: Dennett studied religion as a natural phenomenon.

69261.q: Which event gave New Atheism a strong boost at the start of the 2000s?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The election of a new pope
69261.e: Authors such as Sam Harris saw the attacks as an example of the danger of religious faith. Shortly afterwards, several bestsellers critical of religion appeared.
69261.m: 11 September 2001 gave New Atheism a boost.

69262.q: What mainly distinguishes New Atheism from older atheism?
a: It is outspoken and relies heavily on natural science
It believes in an impersonal creator god
It rejects natural science as a belief
It calls for a new state religion
69262.e: The New Atheists think religion should not just be tolerated but openly criticised. They take their arguments mainly from biology, physics and reason.
69262.m: New Atheism criticises religion outspokenly with scientific arguments.

69263.q: What is meant by agnostic atheism?
a: Not believing in God without claiming certain knowledge
Knowing for certain that there is no God
Believing in God without being able to know him
Believing in many gods without worshipping them
69263.e: Belief and knowledge are two different questions. An agnostic atheist does not believe in God but does not claim to be able to prove that God does not exist.
69263.m: Agnosticism concerns knowledge, atheism concerns belief.

69264.q: What does agnosticism claim about the existence of God?
a: It can be neither proved nor disproved
It is proved for certain by miracles
It has been disproved by science
It is only conceivable in pantheism
69264.e: Agnostics regard the question of God as undecidable. So they withhold judgement instead of believing in God or denying him.
69264.m: Agnostics regard the question of God as unanswerable.

69265.q: Which nickname was Thomas Henry Huxley given because of his defence of the theory of evolution?
69265.e: Huxley defended Darwin’s theory of evolution so energetically in debates that he was called ‘Darwin’s Bulldog’. Darwin himself avoided public debates.

69266.q: What did Thomas Henry Huxley argue about publicly with a bishop in Oxford in 1860?
69266.e: Bishop Samuel Wilberforce mockingly asked about Huxley’s ape ancestors. Huxley’s reply made the debate famous. Huxley later also coined the term ‘agnostic’.
69266.m: In 1860 in Oxford, Huxley defended the theory of evolution.

69267.q: Which language does the word ‘agnostic’ come from, and what does it literally mean?
69267.e: The word combines the negative ‘a’ and ‘gnosis’ (knowledge). Huxley used it to distance himself from the Gnostics, who claimed higher knowledge.

69268.q: Which naturalist wrote in his autobiography that ‘agnostic’ best described his position?
69268.e: Darwin lost his Christian faith over the course of his life. But he did not call himself an atheist; he considered ‘agnostic’ the more fitting term.
69268.m: In later life Charles Darwin saw himself as an agnostic.

69269.q: Which thought experiment did Bertrand Russell invent in 1952 to show where the burden of proof lies for claims about God?
69269.e: Russell said nobody could disprove that a small teapot orbits the Sun. Even so, it is up to the person making the claim to prove it.
69269.m: Russell’s teapot shows that the burden of proof lies with the person making the claim.

69270.q: What does secular humanism base ethics and morality on?
69270.e: Secular humanists reject supernatural explanations. They see humans themselves as responsible for a good life and a fair society.
69270.m: Secular humanism grounds morality without religion.

69271.q: What position do secular humanists take on the relationship between state and religion?
a: They call for a clear separation
They want a single state religion
They demand a ban on all religions
They want churches to be financed by the state
69271.e: Secular humanists stand up for freedom of religion, including freedom from religion. The state should therefore be neutral in matters of belief.
69271.m: Secular humanists call for a neutral state.

69272.q: Which organisation represents people with no religious affiliation and secular humanists in Switzerland?
69272.e: The Freethinkers have campaigned since 1908 for the separation of state and church and for people with no religious affiliation. Pro Helvetia supports culture; Caritas is a Catholic aid organisation.
69272.m: The Freethinkers represent people with no religious affiliation in Switzerland.

69273.q: What is the worldwide umbrella organisation of humanist organisations called today?
69273.e: The organisation was founded in Amsterdam in 1952 and has been called Humanists International since 2019. The World Council of Churches and Religions for Peace are religious organisations.
69273.m: Humanists International is the world organisation of humanists.

69274.q: What is the symbol used by many humanist organisations called?
69274.e: The stylised figure with raised arms was designed by Dennis Barrington in 1965 for the British Humanist Association. It stands for a cheerful, self-determined person.
69274.m: The humanist symbol is called the ‘Happy Human’.

69275.q: What do humanist organisations offer as a replacement for religious rituals?
a: Secular ceremonies for naming, weddings or farewells
Fasting periods following the church year
69275.e: Independent celebrants create ceremonies without reference to God. In this way people with no religious affiliation can also mark important moments in life.
69275.m: Humanists celebrate life’s moments with secular rituals.

69276.q: How does modern humanism describe itself in its principles?
a: As an ethical, rational and democratic life stance
As belief in a punishing God
As a teaching about the fate of the stars
69276.e: This is what the Amsterdam Declaration of Humanists International says. It was adopted in 2002 and renewed in 2022.
69276.m: Humanism sees itself as an ethical, rational and democratic stance.

69277.q: What does the Swiss Freethinkers’ Association mainly campaign for?
a: The separation of state and church
69277.e: The Freethinkers want the state not to favour any religion. They organised themselves in Zurich in 1908.
69277.m: The Swiss Freethinkers call for the separation of state and church.

69278.q: What is the magazine that the Swiss Freethinkers’ Association has published since 2010 called?
69278.e: The quarterly ‘frei denken’ (‘think freely’) succeeded ‘Der Schweizer Freidenker’ in 2010. It appears in three national languages.
69278.m: The magazine of the Swiss Freethinkers is called ‘frei denken’.

69279.q: With which matter do the Swiss Freethinkers help people with template letters?
69279.e: The association supports people who want to leave a national church with explanations and template letters. It campaigns for the separation of state and church.
69279.m: The Swiss Freethinkers support people leaving the church.

69280.q: Which international umbrella organisation does the Swiss Freethinkers’ Association belong to?
69280.e: The Freethinkers are members of Humanists International, the world association of humanist and secular organisations. They also support the Humanist Press Service.
69280.m: The Swiss Freethinkers are part of Humanists International.

69281.q: Which knowledge festival has the Swiss Freethinkers’ Association held about every three years since 2011?
69281.e: Scientists and people from the world of culture appear at the Denkfest (‘thinking festival’). It is the association’s biggest event.
69281.m: The Denkfest is the knowledge festival of the Swiss Freethinkers.

69282.q: Which funding did the Swiss Freethinkers oppose in Lucerne and Valais?
a: The new barracks for the Swiss Guard
The building of a new mosque
69282.e: Public money was to go towards the barracks of the Swiss Guard in the Vatican. The Freethinkers criticised the use of taxpayers’ money for a church institution.
69282.m: The Freethinkers criticise public money for church purposes.

69283.q: Which world view do the Freethinkers hold?
a: A humanist world view without belief in God
A Christian faith without a church
69283.e: Freethinkers rely on reason and science rather than religious revelation. They see themselves as humanists.
69283.m: Freethinkers hold a world view without God.

69284.q: In which year did France separate church and state by law?
69284.e: The law of 1905 guarantees freedom of conscience. Since then the state has neither recognised nor financed any religious community.
69284.m: France separated church and state in 1905.

69285.q: How does Article 1 of the French constitution of 1958 begin?
a: La France est une République indivisible, laïque, démocratique et sociale.
La France est une République libre, chrétienne, unie et sociale.
La France est un État fédéral, neutre, démocratique et social.
La France est une nation laïque, souveraine, libre et unie.
69285.e: Laïcité has been in the French constitution since the constitution of 1946. The constitution of 1958 took over the wording in Article 1.
69285.m: According to its constitution, France is a secular republic.

69286.q: Which area of France is still exempt from the 1905 separation law today?
69286.e: In 1905, Alsace and Moselle belonged to the German Empire. After their return in 1919, the Concordat of 1801 remained in force there, and the state still pays clergy.
69286.m: The Concordat of 1801 still applies in Alsace-Moselle today.

69287.q: What does a French law of 2004 ban in state schools?
69287.e: Pupils at state schools may not wear symbols that conspicuously show a religion. Discreet symbols are still allowed.
69287.m: Since 2004, conspicuous religious symbols have been banned in French state schools.

69288.q: What does the secularism law approved by Geneva’s voters in 2019 require of state representatives in office?
a: Religious neutrality without visible religious symbols
Attending one church service a year
An oath on the Bible on taking office
69288.e: The law modernises Geneva’s secularism, which goes back to the separation of church and state in 1907. Anyone representing the state is to appear religiously neutral and show no religious symbols while in office.
69288.m: Geneva requires religious neutrality from state representatives.

69289.q: How did Swiss voters decide in 1980 on the popular initiative for the complete separation of church and state?
69289.e: On 2 March 1980, only about 21 per cent voted yes. That is why the cantons still regulate the relationship between church and state in Switzerland.
69289.m: In Switzerland, the cantons regulate the relationship between church and state.

69290.q: Which education minister introduced free, compulsory and secular primary schooling in France in 1881/82?
69290.e: Jules Ferry’s laws made primary school free, compulsory and religiously neutral. Religious education was removed from the curriculum of state schools.
69290.m: Jules Ferry made French primary schools secular.

69291.q: According to the FSO, which statement about gender and having no religious affiliation was true for 2022?
a: Men are more often without religious affiliation than women
Women are more often without religious affiliation than men
Only women were asked about it
69291.e: According to the FSO, men more often belong to no religious community than women. So on average, women are slightly more often religiously affiliated.
69291.m: In Switzerland, women are slightly more often religiously affiliated than men.

69292.q: In 2022, roughly what share of the Swiss population aged 15 and over were Evangelical Reformed?
69292.e: According to the FSO, about 21 per cent belonged to the Evangelical Reformed Church in 2022. In the 19th century the Reformed denomination was still the majority denomination in Switzerland.
69292.m: About a fifth of the population is Evangelical Reformed today.

69293.q: With which survey has the FSO determined religious affiliation every year since 2010?
69293.e: Since 2010, an annual sample survey, the structural survey, has replaced the earlier full census. People aged 15 and over are asked.
69293.m: Religious affiliation is now recorded every year with the structural survey.

69294.q: According to the FSO, where was the share of people with no religious affiliation higher in 2022?
69294.e: In 2022 about 36 per cent were without religious affiliation in urban areas, about 28 per cent in rural ones. Cities are more religiously diverse and more secular.
69294.m: Proportionally, more people with no religious affiliation live in cities than in the countryside.

69295.q: Which canton had the lowest share of people with no religious affiliation in 2022, at about 15 per cent?
69295.e: In largely Catholic Appenzell Innerrhoden, only about 15 per cent had no religious affiliation in 2022. In Basel-Stadt and Neuchâtel, by contrast, people with no affiliation are the majority.
69295.m: Rural Catholic cantons have especially few people with no religious affiliation.

69296.q: According to the FSO, roughly what share of the population aged 15 and over was Muslim in 2022?
69296.e: Islamic communities made up about 6 per cent in 2022, about as many as the other Christian communities. Together, the other religious communities make up about 13 per cent.
69296.m: About one person in seventeen in Switzerland belongs to an Islamic community.

69297.q: Up to the 1980s, how large was the combined share of the two major national churches?
69297.e: Until the 1980s, over 90 per cent of the population belonged to the Reformed or the Catholic Church. Today it is only just over half.
69297.m: The national churches have lost a large part of their members within a few decades.

69298.q: Which FSO survey asks in depth about religious practice and spirituality every five years?
a: The Survey on Language, Religion and Culture
69298.e: The Survey on Language, Religion and Culture (ESRK) complements the structural survey. It asks, for example, about church attendance, prayer and beliefs.
69298.m: The ESRK shows how people in Switzerland live their faith in everyday life.

69299.q: Which provision about clothing in public spaces did voters add to the Federal Constitution in 2021?
69299.e: On 7 March 2021, about 51.2 per cent accepted the initiative ‘Yes to a ban on face coverings’. The debate focused strongly on the burqa and niqab.
69299.m: Since 2021 the Federal Constitution has contained a ban on face coverings.

69300.q: What does paragraph 4 of Article 15 of the Federal Constitution mainly guarantee?
a: Nobody may be forced into religion
Every municipality must have a church
Religious education is compulsory for all
69300.e: Paragraph 4 states that nobody may be forced to join a religious community, to perform a religious act or to attend religious education. This is called negative freedom of religion.
69300.m: Freedom of religion also includes the right to belong to no religion.

69301.q: Under the Civil Code, from what age does a child decide on their religious affiliation themselves?
69301.e: Under Article 303 paragraph 3 of the Civil Code, a child who has reached the age of 16 decides independently on their religious affiliation. This is called religious majority.
69301.m: In Switzerland you come of age in religious matters at 16.

69302.q: Which denominational exception article, which made new dioceses subject to federal approval, was abolished in 2001?
69302.e: The diocese article dated from the time of the Kulturkampf. In 2001 voters removed it from the Federal Constitution, the last of these denominational exception articles.
69302.m: With the diocese article, the last Kulturkampf article fell in 2001.

69303.q: Which provision was added to Article 72 of the Federal Constitution in 2009 by a popular initiative?
69303.e: On 29 November 2009, about 57.5 per cent of voters accepted the minaret initiative. Since then Article 72 paragraph 3 of the Constitution has stated that building minarets is prohibited.
69303.m: Since 2009 the Federal Constitution has banned the building of new minarets.

69304.q: Which denominational exception ban was removed from the Constitution in a popular vote in 1973?
69304.e: From 1848 the Federal Constitution banned the Jesuit order, and in 1874 a ban on new monasteries was added. Both exception articles were abolished by voters in 1973.
69304.m: Lifting the ban on the Jesuits in 1973 ended a legacy of the Kulturkampf.

69305.q: According to Article 36 of the Federal Constitution, under what condition may the state restrict a fundamental right such as freedom of religion?
a: With a legal basis and proportionality
Only with the consent of all churches
Only in wartime, without a law
At any time by a decision of a municipality
69305.e: Restrictions need a legal basis, a public interest or the protection of the fundamental rights of others, and they must be proportionate. The core content remains inviolable.
69305.m: Freedom of religion can also be restricted, but only under strict conditions.

69306.q: What was the European Court of Human Rights’ 2017 judgment against Switzerland in the case of Osmanoğlu and Kocabaş about?
69306.e: Muslim parents from Basel wanted their daughters to be excused from mixed swimming lessons. The Court found that the duty to take part did not violate freedom of religion, because integration at school outweighed it.
69306.m: According to the ECtHR, compulsory schooling can outweigh a religious request for exemption.

69307.q: Which group of people in Switzerland only gained the right to settle freely in 1866, through a popular vote?
69307.e: The Federal Constitution of 1848 granted freedom of settlement and worship only to Christians. Jews gained freedom of settlement in 1866 and full freedom of belief and worship with the constitution of 1874.
69307.m: In Switzerland, freedom of belief only applied to everyone from 1874.

69308.q: What does the classic secularisation thesis claim?
a: Modernisation leads to religion losing importance
Religion becomes ever stronger with modernity
69308.e: The classic thesis assumes that industrialisation, science and pluralisation reduce the social importance of religion. It shaped the sociology of religion until the 1970s.
69308.m: The secularisation thesis links modernisation with religion losing importance.

69309.q: Which observation speaks against the classic secularisation thesis?
a: In modern countries like the USA, religion remains strong
In Europe fewer people go to church
Many people leave the national churches
There are more people with no religious affiliation in cities
69309.e: The USA is highly modern and yet very religious. Religion is also growing in many places worldwide. That is why Europe is now seen more as the exception.
69309.m: The USA shows that modernity does not always mean less religion.

69310.q: What does the sociologist Grace Davie’s formula ‘believing without belonging’ mean?
a: People believe without actively belonging to a church
People belong to a church without believing
69310.e: Davie observed in Britain that many people believe in something but hardly take part in church life. The formula became a catchphrase of the sociology of religion.
69310.m: Believing without belonging describes many people in Europe.

69311.q: Which idea is at the centre of Thomas Luckmann’s book ‘The Invisible Religion’?
a: Religion becomes private rather than church-based
Religion becomes a task of the state
69311.e: Luckmann argued that religion does not disappear but moves out of the churches into the private search for meaning. He therefore spoke of the privatisation of religion.
69311.m: According to Luckmann, religion becomes invisible in modernity but not meaningless.

69312.q: What is meant by ‘differentiation’ as part of secularisation?
a: Areas such as politics, school and science break away from the church
The churches split into many small groups
The state takes over the leadership of the churches
69312.e: In the past, the church also shaped school, law and science. In modern times these areas follow their own rules. This development is regarded as a well-documented part of secularisation.
69312.m: Secularisation also means that areas of society break away from the church.

69313.q: How do Pippa Norris and Ronald Inglehart explain the decline of religiosity in ‘Sacred and Secular’?
a: With a lack of church buildings
69313.e: Norris and Inglehart show that religiosity declines where people are economically and socially secure. In insecure living conditions, religion stays more important.
69313.m: According to Norris and Inglehart, religion loses importance where life becomes more secure.

69314.q: Which approach by Rodney Stark explains religious vitality through competition in a religious market?
69314.e: Stark and others applied economic models to religion: many competing providers, as in the USA, lead to high participation. State churches with a monopoly, by contrast, tend to create passivity.
69314.m: Market theory sees religious diversity as a driver of religious activity.

69315.q: Which philosopher coined the term ‘post-secular society’ after 2001?
69315.e: Jürgen Habermas spoke of a post-secular society in his 2001 Peace Prize speech ‘Faith and Knowledge’. He meant that secular societies must adjust to the continued existence of religion.
69315.m: Habermas calls a society post-secular if it expects religion to live on.

69316.q: Which sociologist coined the expression ‘the disenchantment of the world’?
69316.e: Max Weber thought that in modern times all things could in principle be mastered by calculation. Mysterious, incalculable powers no longer played a role.
69316.m: The disenchantment of the world is a term coined by Max Weber.

69317.q: Which overarching process of modernity is closely linked to disenchantment in Max Weber’s work?
