69317.e: For Weber, disenchantment is part of a comprehensive rationalisation of science, economy, law and administration. Magical means are replaced by technical means and calculation.
69317.m: For Weber, disenchantment is part of the rationalisation of the world.

69318.q: According to Weber’s ‘Protestant Ethic’, which teaching of Calvin caused a special inner unrest among believers?
69318.e: According to the doctrine of predestination, God has decided in advance who will be saved. Weber thought Calvinists therefore looked for a sign of being chosen in success at work.
69318.m: The doctrine of predestination is central to Weber’s thesis on Protestantism.

69319.q: What did Max Weber call the disciplined way of life, far from pleasure, within a worldly occupation?
69319.e: Inner-worldly asceticism demands self-control and hard work in the midst of the world, instead of withdrawal into a monastery. According to Weber, it encouraged the spirit of capitalism.
69319.m: Inner-worldly asceticism means being devout through disciplined work in everyday life.

69320.q: In which years did Weber’s essay ‘The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism’ first appear?
69320.e: The essay appeared in two parts in 1904 and 1905 in the ‘Archiv für Sozialwissenschaft und Sozialpolitik’. Weber revised it in 1920, shortly before his death.
69320.m: Weber’s study of Protestantism appeared in 1904 and 1905.

69321.q: Which image did Weber use at the end of the ‘Protestant Ethic’ for the compelling order of the modern economy?
69321.e: Weber wrote that the concern for external goods had become a ‘shell as hard as steel’. Talcott Parsons translated the image as ‘iron cage’.
69321.m: For Weber, the iron cage stands for the constraints of rationalised modernity.

69322.q: In Weber’s work, which form of legitimate authority rests on the extraordinary appeal of a person?
69322.e: Weber distinguished traditional, legal and charismatic authority. Charisma refers to a gift regarded as extraordinary, such as is attributed to prophets or founders of religions.
69322.m: Charismatic authority rests on belief in a special person.

69323.q: According to Max Weber, what distinguishes a sect from a church?
a: You join it consciously and voluntarily
It is recognised by the state
It has no teaching of its own
69323.e: You are usually born into a church. According to Weber, you join a sect consciously and have to prove yourself worthy.
69323.m: Church and sect differ in the kind of membership.

69324.q: Why does religious studies prefer the term ‘new religious movement’ to ‘sect’ or ‘cult’?
a: It only applies to Christian groups
It only refers to banned groups
69324.e: In everyday use, ‘sect’ or ‘cult’ is derogatory and used inconsistently. The term ‘new religious movement’ describes groups without prejudice; most arose in the 19th or 20th century.
69324.m: New religious movement is a neutral technical term in religious studies.

69325.q: What is the task of specialist centres such as infoSekta in Switzerland?
a: To give factual information and advice about religious groups
To give new religions state approval
69325.e: Such centres advise those affected and their relatives and collect information. In Britain, INFORM does similar work.
69325.m: Specialist centres give factual information about new religious movements.

69326.q: Who founded Scientology, which is based on the 1950 book ‘Dianetics’?
69326.e: L. Ron Hubbard published ‘Dianetics’ in 1950 and founded the first Church of Scientology in the USA in 1954. The organisation is controversial in several countries.
69326.m: Scientology goes back to L. Ron Hubbard.

69327.q: Which expression was common in the German-speaking world in the 1970s for new movements with many young members?
69327.e: The Protestant commissioner for sects Friedrich-Wilhelm Haack made the term ‘youth religions’ (Jugendreligionen) known. Today it is regarded as inaccurate, because the members grew older.
69327.m: Youth religions was an older expression for new religious movements.

69328.q: Which group lost many members through murder and suicide in Cheiry (Fribourg) and Salvan (Valais) in 1994?
a: The Order of the Solar Temple
69328.e: In October 1994, 48 members of the Order of the Solar Temple died in Switzerland, and others in Canada. The tragedy led to political debates about how to deal with controlling groups.
69328.m: The Solar Temple tragedy of 1994 shook Switzerland.

69329.q: Who founded the Unification Church in Seoul in 1954?
69329.e: Sun Myung Moon founded the Unification Church in South Korea in 1954. The movement became known among other things for its mass weddings.
69329.m: The Unification Church comes from South Korea.

69330.q: Where did more than 900 members of Jim Jones’s ‘Peoples Temple’ die in 1978?
69330.e: In November 1978, more than 900 people died in the Jonestown settlement in Guyana, many from poisoned drinks. The event strongly shaped the image of dangerous groups.
69330.m: Jonestown is regarded as one of the greatest tragedies involving a religious group.

69331.q: Which Japanese group carried out a poison gas attack on the Tokyo underground in 1995?
69331.e: In March 1995, members of Aum Shinrikyo released the nerve gas sarin on the Tokyo underground. Several people died and thousands were injured.
69331.m: The 1995 sarin attack was carried out by Aum Shinrikyo.

a: A specialist centre for questions about sects
69332.e: infoSekta was founded in Zurich in 1990. It gives information and advice on sects, controlling groups and world views.
69332.m: Since 1990, infoSekta has given advice on questions about sects and world views.

69333.q: What position does infoSekta take towards religious communities?
a: It is independent of any denomination
It belongs to the Reformed Church
It is a Catholic religious order’s office
69333.e: infoSekta describes itself as a specialist centre independent of any denomination. It judges groups by their behaviour, not by their beliefs.
69333.m: infoSekta works independently of churches and religious communities.

69334.q: What legal form does infoSekta have?
69334.e: infoSekta is organised as an association and is based in Zurich. It offers information, advice, prevention and further training.
69334.m: infoSekta is run by an association.

69335.q: Among others, whom is infoSekta’s advice especially aimed at?
a: Relatives and people who have left groups
69335.e: infoSekta advises those affected, relatives, people who have left groups and professionals, for example from schools. The aim is to defuse conflicts around controlling groups.
69335.m: Worried relatives can also get advice from infoSekta.

69336.q: Which centre in French-speaking Switzerland has carried out similar tasks to infoSekta since the early 2000s?
a: The Centre intercantonal d’information sur les croyances
69336.e: The CIC in Geneva was set up after the Solar Temple tragedy and is supported by several cantons of French-speaking Switzerland and Ticino. It gives neutral information about faith communities.
69336.m: In French-speaking Switzerland, the CIC provides information about religious groups.

69337.q: Which committee of the National Council published a report on ‘sects or controlling movements in Switzerland’ in 1999?
69337.e: After the Solar Temple tragedy, the National Council’s Control Committee examined whether the state should act more strongly. The report used the term ‘controlling movements’.
69337.m: The Control Committee’s 1999 report brought the topic of sects to the federal parliament.

69338.q: Unlike infoSekta, who runs the Protestant information centre on churches, sects and religions (relinfo)?
69338.e: relinfo in Rüti (Zurich) works from a Reformed Protestant perspective. infoSekta, by contrast, is independent of any denomination.
69338.m: Besides infoSekta, there are also church information centres on questions about sects.

69339.q: By which criterion do specialist centres like infoSekta mainly judge a group?
a: By how it treats its members
By the size of its buildings
By the age of its teaching
69339.e: What matters is problematic behaviour such as strong dependency, isolation or pressure when leaving. An unusual belief alone does not make a group problematic.
69339.m: A group is problematic because of its behaviour, not because of its beliefs.

69340.q: What does the Greek word from which ‘esoteric’ is derived mean?
69340.e: ‘Esoterikos’ means belonging within, that is, reserved for an inner circle of initiates. The opposite is ‘exoteric’, meant for the public.
69340.m: Esoteric originally means meant only for an inner circle.

69341.q: Who founded the Theosophical Society in New York in 1875 with Henry Steel Olcott?
69341.e: Helena Petrovna Blavatsky combined Western esotericism with ideas from Hinduism and Buddhism. Theosophy influenced many later esoteric movements.
69341.m: Modern Theosophy goes back to Helena Blavatsky.

69342.q: In which Swiss municipality is the Goetheanum, the centre of anthroposophy?
69342.e: Rudolf Steiner had the first Goetheanum built in Dornach (Solothurn); it burnt down on New Year’s Eve 1922. Today’s concrete building was completed in 1928.
69342.m: The Goetheanum in Dornach is the headquarters of anthroposophy.

69343.q: Which settlement near Ascona became a centre of the life reform movement and alternative spirituality around 1900?
69343.e: Around 1900, dropouts founded a vegetarian colony on Monte Verità. Later, artists, dancers and thinkers came from all over Europe.
69343.m: Monte Verità near Ascona was a meeting place of the life reform movement.

69344.q: Which astrological age does the New Age movement refer to?
69344.e: New Age expects a new age of consciousness linked to the transition from the Age of Pisces to the Age of Aquarius. The movement flourished above all in the 1970s and 1980s.
69344.m: New Age expects the Age of Aquarius.

69345.q: Which esoteric practice interprets the position of the stars at birth to describe a person’s character?
69345.e: Astrology assumes that the stars and human lives correspond to each other. Astronomy, by contrast, is the natural science of celestial bodies.
69345.m: Astrology interprets the stars; astronomy studies them.

69346.q: What do people mean when they describe themselves as ‘spiritual but not religious’?
a: They look for meaning and spirituality outside the churches
They reject every form of belief
They strictly belong to a church
They believe only in natural science
69346.e: Many people break away from churches but keep looking for meaning, for example in meditation or experiences of nature. Researchers speak of a shift towards personal spirituality.
69346.m: Spirituality also exists outside the churches.

69347.q: According to the FSO Survey on Language, Religion and Culture 2014, how many people with no religious affiliation in Switzerland believed in a higher power?
69347.e: In 2014, 31 per cent of people with no religious affiliation said they believed in a higher power, and just over 40 per cent believed in gifts such as healing or clairvoyance. So having no religious affiliation does not always mean having no belief.
69347.m: Many people with no religious affiliation still have spiritual ideas.

69348.q: Under the Labour Act, how many public holidays at most may the cantons treat in the same way as Sundays?
69348.e: Under Article 20a paragraph 1 of the Labour Act, the cantons may treat at most eight further holidays a year like Sundays. The National Day comes on top of that.
69348.m: Besides 1 August, each canton has at most eight public holidays under labour law.

69349.q: Under the Labour Act, which public holiday is treated like a Sunday throughout Switzerland?
69349.e: Article 20a of the Labour Act treats only the National Day like a Sunday throughout Switzerland. The cantons set the other public holidays.
69349.m: Only 1 August is a public holiday everywhere under federal law.

69350.q: In Switzerland, can you take time off on a religious holiday that your canton does not recognise?
a: Yes, if you tell your employer in advance
Only as a member of a national church
69350.e: Article 20a of the Labour Act allows people to stay away from work on other religious holidays. You must give notice at least three days in advance.
69350.m: Anyone who wants to celebrate their own religious holiday must give notice in advance.

69351.q: What may the employer require if someone is absent on a religious holiday not recognised by the canton?
a: That the working time is made up
69351.e: Article 20a refers to Article 11 of the Labour Act: the lost working time can be worked in advance or made up afterwards. But the employer may not forbid the absence.
69351.m: Time taken for your own religious holiday usually has to be made up.

69352.q: Under the Labour Act, what must the employer grant on request where possible?
a: A holiday bonus of 50 per cent
69352.e: Article 20a paragraph 3 of the Labour Act obliges employers to give employees time off for religious ceremonies where possible. If attendance is possible during a break, no extra time has to be given.
69352.m: Employers must allow attendance at religious ceremonies where possible.

69353.q: Since a popular vote in which year has 1 August been a work-free public holiday throughout Switzerland?
69353.e: In 1993 voters accepted the initiative for a work-free National Day. Since 1994, 1 August has been a day off work throughout Switzerland.
69353.m: Since 1994, 1 August has been a day off work everywhere in Switzerland.

69354.q: In which two cantons is Good Friday not a general public holiday?
69354.e: Good Friday is a public holiday in almost all cantons, but not in Ticino and Valais. Originally it was a major holiday mainly for the Reformed.
69354.m: Good Friday is not a public holiday only in Ticino and Valais.

69355.q: Which law in principle prohibits employing workers on a Sunday?
69355.e: Article 18 of the Labour Act prohibits Sunday work; exceptions need a permit. Sunday rest has Christian roots but today is justified on social grounds.
69355.m: The Labour Act protects Sunday rest.

69356.q: Why does Ramadan move about eleven days earlier in the solar calendar each year?
a: The Islamic lunar year has about 354 days
Ramadan is chosen afresh every year
69356.e: The Islamic calendar is a purely lunar calendar with twelve months and about 354 days. Because it has no leap months, the festivals move through all the seasons.
69356.m: Islamic festivals move because the lunar year is shorter than the solar year.

69357.q: How does the Jewish calendar keep lunar months and the solar year in step?
a: With seven leap months in 19 years
With a leap day every four years
With a leap year every 100 years
69357.e: The Jewish calendar is a lunisolar calendar. In 19 years, seven leap years with an extra month of Adar are added, so that Passover stays in spring.
69357.m: The Jewish calendar adds leap months so that the festivals stay in their season.

69358.q: Which year number does the Jewish calendar count from the New Year festival in autumn 2025?
69358.e: The Jewish count begins with the traditionally calculated creation of the world. With Rosh Hashanah in September 2025, the year 5786 began.
69358.m: The Jewish calendar counts the years since the creation of the world.

69359.q: Why do many Orthodox churches celebrate Christmas on 7 January?
a: They count Christmas from New Year
They only celebrate the baptism of Jesus
69359.e: The Julian calendar is currently 13 days behind the Gregorian one. So 25 December in the Julian calendar corresponds to 7 January in the Gregorian calendar.
69359.m: Orthodox Christmas on 7 January results from the Julian calendar.

69360.q: By which rule has the Christian date of Easter been calculated since the Council of Nicaea?
a: First Sunday after the first full moon of spring
Second Sunday after the new moon in April
First Sunday after the summer solstice
69360.e: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon from the start of spring. That is why, in the West, Easter falls between 22 March and 25 April.
69360.m: The date of Easter depends on the first full moon of spring.

69361.q: How is the Baha’i calendar structured?
a: 19 months of 19 days each, plus extra days
69361.e: The Badi calendar has 19 months of 19 days, which makes 361 days, plus four or five inserted days. New Year, Naw-Ruz, falls at the start of spring.
69361.m: The number 19 plays a central role in the Baha’i calendar.

69362.q: Why does the Buddhist festival of Vesak fall on a different date each year, usually in May?
a: It is set by the Dalai Lama
It always falls on a Monday
69362.e: In many countries, Vesak is celebrated at the full moon of the month of Vesakha, which usually falls in May. The festival commemorates the birth, enlightenment and death of the Buddha.
69362.m: Many religious festivals follow the moon.

69363.q: Which regions do most Muslims in Switzerland originally come from?
69363.e: Many came from the former Yugoslavia and Turkey as labour migrants from the 1960s and as war refugees in the 1990s. Many come from Kosovo, North Macedonia and Bosnia.
69363.m: Islam in Switzerland is strongly shaped by the Balkans and Turkey.

69364.q: Which group, fleeing civil war from the 1980s onwards, brought many Hindu temples to Switzerland?
69364.e: Since the civil war in Sri Lanka from 1983, many Tamils have come to Switzerland. They form the largest Hindu community in the country.
69364.m: Hinduism in Switzerland is mainly Tamil.

69365.q: Which religious refugees came to Switzerland in large numbers after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685?
69365.e: After 1685, French Protestants, the Huguenots, fled to Reformed areas such as Geneva, Bern and Zurich. Among other things, they promoted watchmaking and the textile trade.
69365.m: After 1685, Huguenots shaped the economy of Reformed Swiss towns.

69366.q: What are the Catholic pastoral centres in Switzerland for believers who speak other languages, such as Italians or Portuguese, called?
69366.e: With labour migration after the Second World War, foreign-language missions were set up, at first mainly Italian ones. Today they exist in many languages.

69367.q: Where was a Buddhist monastery founded in Switzerland in 1968 after Tibetan refugees were taken in?
a: In Rikon in the Töss valley
69367.e: Switzerland took in refugees from Tibet from the 1960s. The Tibet Institute was founded for them in Rikon (Zurich) in 1968.
69367.m: The Tibet Institute in Rikon was founded for Tibetan refugees.

69368.q: Which Christian family of churches has grown in Switzerland mainly through immigration from Eastern Europe, the Balkans and Eritrea?
69368.e: Serbian, Romanian, Russian and Eritrean Orthodox congregations arose mainly through migration. Their services are often held in the language of the country of origin.
69368.m: Orthodoxy in Switzerland is a church of migration.

69369.q: What does the term ‘migrant church’ mean?
a: A church without a fixed building for tourists
A church for hikers in the Alps
69369.e: Migrant churches are Christian congregations founded by immigrants themselves, often with an African, Latin American or Asian background. They often rent premises from the national churches.
69369.m: Migrant churches enrich the Christian landscape of Switzerland.

69370.q: What does the term ‘diaspora’ mean in religious studies?
a: A religious community far from its region of origin
A community that only lives in its country of origin
A new church after a split
69370.e: Diaspora is Greek for scattering and first referred to Jews outside Israel. Today the term generally describes communities that practise their religion far from their region of origin.
69370.m: In the diaspora, religion often becomes a link to the old homeland.

69371.q: Which series of publications from 1910 to 1915 does the term ‘fundamentalism’ go back to?
69371.e: Conservative Protestants in the USA defended the foundations of the faith against liberal theology in the series ‘The Fundamentals’. So the term arose in a Christian setting.
69371.m: The term fundamentalism comes from American Protestantism.

69372.q: In which country did the term ‘fundamentalism’ arise?
69372.e: Conservative Protestants in the USA called themselves fundamentalists from 1920. Only later was the term applied to other religions.
69372.m: Fundamentalist was first a name American Protestants gave themselves.

69373.q: Which teaching about the Bible is central to Protestant fundamentalism?
69373.e: Fundamentalists regard the Bible as without error in all its statements, including those about history and nature. They reject historical-critical interpretation of the Bible.
69373.m: For fundamentalists, the Bible is free of error in every statement.

69374.q: What was the Scopes Trial of 1925 in Tennessee about?
69374.e: The teacher John Scopes was charged because he had taught the theory of evolution. The trial became a symbol of the conflict between fundamentalism and modern science.
69374.m: The Scopes Trial shows the dispute over evolution and the Bible.

69375.q: How does the sociology of religion, for example Martin Riesebrodt, interpret fundamentalism?
a: As a modern reaction to modernity
As the unchanged original form of every religion
As a preliminary stage of atheism
69375.e: Fundamentalism is not simply clinging to old tradition but a modern protest movement against secularisation and pluralism. In doing so it uses modern means such as mass media itself.
69375.m: Fundamentalism is a child of modernity that turns against it.

69376.q: Which research project of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences compared fundamentalisms in many religions from 1987 to 1995?
69376.e: Under the direction of Martin E. Marty and R. Scott Appleby, several volumes appeared on fundamentalisms in Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism and other religions. In this way the term came to be used comparatively.
69376.m: The Fundamentalism Project applied the term to many religions.

69377.q: Which event of 1979 made the term fundamentalism known worldwide in connection with Islam too?
a: The fall of the Berlin Wall
The founding of the Arab League
69377.e: With the revolution under Ayatollah Khomeini, a Shiite theocracy came into being in 1979. Western media then applied the term fundamentalism to Islamic movements.
69377.m: Since 1979 the term fundamentalism has also been applied to Islam.

69378.q: Which position rejects the biological theory of evolution for religious reasons and is often linked with fundamentalism?
69378.e: Creationism understands the biblical creation story as a literal account. Young Earth creationists think the Earth is only a few thousand years old.
69378.m: Creationism interprets the creation story literally.

69379.q: In which city did Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar sign the Document on Human Fraternity in 2019?
69379.e: On 4 February 2019, Pope Francis and Ahmad al-Tayyeb signed the joint declaration in Abu Dhabi. The UN later declared 4 February the International Day of Human Fraternity.
69379.m: The Document on Human Fraternity was signed in Abu Dhabi in 2019.

69380.q: What is the difference between a multi-religious and an interreligious prayer?
a: People pray side by side instead of with shared words
People pray in only one language
People pray only in a church
69380.e: In a multi-religious prayer, each religion prays in turn in its own way, while the others are respectfully present. In an interreligious prayer, everyone says one text together.
69380.m: Multi-religious means praying side by side; interreligious means praying together.

69381.q: Since when has the Swiss Confederation celebrated a common day of prayer by decision of the Diet?
69381.e: In 1832 the Diet decided on a common day of thanksgiving, repentance and prayer for Catholic and Reformed cantons. It is celebrated on the third Sunday in September and today is often interreligious.
69381.m: Since 1832, the Federal Day of Thanksgiving, Repentance and Prayer has united the denominations.

69382.q: In which city did the first Parliament of the World’s Religions take place in 1893?
69382.e: The Parliament of the World’s Religions met in 1893 during the World’s Fair in Chicago. Swami Vivekananda made Hinduism known in the West there.
69382.m: Modern interreligious dialogue began in Chicago in 1893.

69383.q: Which declaration of the Second Vatican Council of 1965 honours other religions and paved the way for joint celebrations?
69383.e: ‘Nostra aetate’ declares that the Catholic Church rejects nothing that is true and holy in other religions. The declaration also condemns antisemitism.
69383.m: With Nostra aetate, the Catholic Church opened itself to dialogue with other religions.

69384.q: Which week did the UN General Assembly declare in 2010, on Jordan’s proposal, for the first week of February?
69384.e: World Interfaith Harmony Week goes back to a proposal by King Abdullah II of Jordan. Religious communities worldwide organise joint events during this week.
69384.m: The UN World Interfaith Harmony Week takes place at the start of February each year.

69385.q: What is the task of the Interreligious Working Group in Switzerland (IRAS COTIS)?
a: To promote dialogue between the religions
To give new religions state approval
69385.e: IRAS COTIS was founded in 1992 as a national network. Among other things, it organises the Week of Religions.
69385.m: IRAS COTIS promotes interreligious exchange in Switzerland.

69386.q: What are Judaism, Christianity and Islam called together when, at celebrations, they refer to a common forefather?
69386.e: All three religions see Abraham as a forefather of faith. Many trialogue celebrations and conversations refer to this.
69386.m: Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called Abrahamic religions.

69387.q: On which occasions are interreligious memorial services held especially often in Switzerland?
69387.e: After accidents with victims of different backgrounds, several religious communities often organise memorial services together. In this way all those affected can mourn in their own tradition.
69387.m: Interreligious memorial services give mourners of different religions a shared space.

69388.q: Which country does the healing method Reiki, widespread in the esoteric scene, come from?
69388.e: Reiki goes back to the Japanese Mikao Usui, who taught it in the 1920s. No medical effect beyond the placebo effect has been scientifically proven.
69388.m: Reiki is an esoteric practice that comes from Japan.

69389.q: For the philosopher Charles Taylor, what does ‘secular’ mainly mean?
a: Belief is one option among several
Churches are run by the state
69389.e: Taylor asks why around 1500 it was almost impossible not to believe in God, whereas today it is easy. For him, secular means that belief can no longer be taken for granted.
69389.m: For Charles Taylor, belief today is one option among several.

69391.q: Which Persian king allowed the Jews to return from the Babylonian Exile after conquering Babylon in 539 BC?
69391.e: Cyrus II conquered Babylon and allowed the exiles to return home and rebuild the Temple. But many Jews stayed in Babylonia, which became a centre of the diaspora.
69391.m: Cyrus II ended the Babylonian Exile.

69392.q: After which failed revolt from AD 132 to 135 were Jews no longer allowed to enter Jerusalem?
69392.e: Emperor Hadrian crushed the revolt led by Simon bar Kokhba, refounded Jerusalem as Aelia Capitolina and banned Jews from entering. After that, the diaspora became the main form of Jewish life.
69392.m: After the Bar Kokhba revolt, the Jews were banished from Jerusalem.

69393.q: In which diaspora city was the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, produced?
69393.e: The large Jewish community in Alexandria in Egypt spoke Greek. There the Torah was translated into Greek from the 3rd century BC.
69393.m: The Septuagint was translated in Alexandria.

69394.q: Roughly what share of all Jews worldwide live in Israel today (as of 2024)?
69394.e: Of about 15.7 million Jews worldwide, about 7.2 million live in Israel, so just under half. The rest live in the diaspora, mainly in the USA.
69394.m: Just over half of all Jews today live outside Israel.

69395.q: In which Egyptian city did one of the largest Jewish communities of antiquity live, where the Torah was translated into Greek?
69395.e: Many Greek-speaking Jews lived in Alexandria. The Greek translation of the Bible, the Septuagint, was produced there.
69395.m: Alexandria was a major centre of the Jewish diaspora.

69396.q: Which event in the 6th century BC led to the first large Jewish community outside the Land of Israel?
a: The destruction of the Second Temple
69396.e: After Jerusalem was conquered in 587 BC, many Jews were deported to Babylon. A large community remained there even after the exile.
69396.m: The Jewish diaspora began with the Babylonian Exile.

69397.q: In which country does the largest Jewish community outside Israel live today?
69397.e: About six million Jews live in the USA. That is almost as many as in Israel.
69397.m: The largest diaspora community lives in the USA.

69398.q: Which area does the Hebrew word ‘Sefarad’, from which the name Sephardim comes, refer to?
69398.e: Sefarad is a biblical place name that in the Middle Ages was applied to Spain and Portugal. Sephardim are the descendants of the Jews of the Iberian Peninsula.
69398.m: Sephardim are descended from the Jews of Spain and Portugal.

69399.q: Which traditional language did many Sephardim speak after their expulsion?
69399.e: Ladino, or Judaeo-Spanish, is based on Old Spanish with Hebrew, Turkish and other influences. For a long time it was written in Hebrew script.
69399.m: Ladino is the language of the Sephardic Jews.

69400.q: Which empire took in especially many expelled Sephardim after 1492, for example in Thessaloniki?
69400.e: Sultan Bayezid II allowed the refugees to settle in the Ottoman Empire. For centuries afterwards, Thessaloniki had a Jewish majority population.
69400.m: The Ottoman Empire became the new home of many Sephardim.

69401.q: What were Jews on the Iberian Peninsula called who were forcibly baptised but secretly kept Jewish customs?
69401.e: Many Jews had themselves baptised under pressure but secretly went on living by Jewish tradition. The Inquisition persecuted them harshly.
69401.m: Marranos were forcibly baptised Jews who secretly lived as Jews.

69402.q: Which area did the Hebrew word “Ashkenaz” refer to in the Middle Ages?
69402.e: In medieval Hebrew, Ashkenaz stood for Germany, especially the Rhineland. Ashkenazim are Jews with Central and Eastern European roots.
69402.m: Ashkenaz was the Hebrew name for the German lands.

69403.q: What are Speyer, Worms and Mainz known for in Jewish history?
a: As early centres of Jewish learning in the Middle Ages
As venues of the first Zionist Congresses
As seat of the High Council (Sanhedrin)
69403.e: The three Rhine cities, called ShUM in Hebrew, were important centres of Ashkenazi Judaism in the Middle Ages. Since 2021 they have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
69403.m: Speyer, Worms and Mainz were centres of Jewish learning.

69404.q: Where did many Ashkenazi Jews emigrate to after the persecutions of the late Middle Ages?
69404.e: Polish rulers granted Jews privileges of protection. So Poland-Lithuania became the centre of Ashkenazi Judaism until the 20th century.
69404.m: Poland-Lithuania became the heartland of the Ashkenazim.

69405.q: Which devout movement did Israel ben Eliezer, known as the Baal Shem Tov, found in Eastern Europe in the 18th century?
69405.e: Hasidism stresses joy, prayer and closeness to God in everyday life. It spread quickly among the Ashkenazi Jews of Eastern Europe.
69405.m: The Baal Shem Tov is regarded as the founder of Hasidism.

69406.q: In which script is Yiddish traditionally written?
69406.e: Yiddish uses the Hebrew alphabet and is written from right to left. Unlike in Hebrew, the vowels are usually written out.
69406.m: Yiddish is written with Hebrew letters.

69408.q: What does the word “chutzpah”, which comes from Yiddish, mean?
69408.e: Chutzpah describes a mixture of cheek and brazenness. The word goes back to Hebrew.

69409.q: Which author writing in Yiddish received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1978?
69409.e: Isaac Bashevis Singer wrote his novels and stories in Yiddish. He is still the only Nobel laureate who wrote in that language.
69409.m: Isaac Bashevis Singer won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1978 for his Yiddish work.

69410.q: The musical “Fiddler on the Roof” about Tevye the milkman is based on stories by which Yiddish writer?
69410.e: Sholem Aleichem wrote the stories of “Tevye the Milkman” in Yiddish. The musical “Fiddler on the Roof” came out in 1964.
69410.m: Fiddler on the Roof goes back to stories by Sholem Aleichem.

69411.q: Which language is most of the Yiddish vocabulary based on?
69411.e: Yiddish developed in the Middle Ages from German dialects. Words from Hebrew, Aramaic and Slavic languages were added.

69412.q: Which Western Yiddish dialect was spoken in the canton of Aargau until the 20th century?
69412.e: The rural Jewish population in the Surb valley spoke its own form of Western Yiddish. After many families moved to the cities, the dialect died out.
69412.m: In Aargau, Surbtal Yiddish was once spoken.

69413.q: Roughly how many people spoke Yiddish before the Holocaust?
69413.e: Before the Second World War, Yiddish was the everyday language of around 11 to 13 million people. The Holocaust destroyed most of this language community.
69413.m: Before the Holocaust, over ten million people spoke Yiddish.

69414.q: With which letters is Yiddish traditionally written?
69414.e: Yiddish is closely related to German but is written with the Hebrew alphabet. It was the everyday language of many Jews in Central and Eastern Europe.
69414.m: Yiddish is written with Hebrew letters.

69415.q: To which condominium (Gemeine Herrschaft) of the Swiss Confederates did Endingen and Lengnau belong in the 18th century?
69415.e: The County of Baden was governed jointly by several Confederate cantons. The Jews regularly had to buy expensive letters of protection from the bailiffs.
69415.m: Endingen and Lengnau were in the County of Baden.

69416.q: Why do many old houses in Endingen and Lengnau have two front doors side by side?
a: Jews and Christians were not allowed to use a shared entrance
Each door led to a different stable
One door was only for holidays
The tax depended on the number of doors
69416.e: Jews and Christians were not supposed to live under the same roof. Two separate entrances got round this rule; they are called double-door houses.
69416.m: The double-door houses in the Surbtal bear witness to the separation of Jews and Christians.

69417.q: What is the attack on the Jews of Endingen and Lengnau in September 1802 called?
69417.e: Over 800 men from neighbouring villages looted Jewish houses, while Christians were spared. The name comes from the time of the plum harvest.
69417.m: The Plum War of 1802 was an attack on the Surbtal Jews.

69418.q: What is the significance of the synagogue in Lengnau established in 1750?
a: first Jewish house of worship of the modern era in Switzerland
69418.e: With the building of 1750, the Jews of Lengnau got their own house of worship. Today's building in the round-arch style by Ferdinand Stadler dates from 1847.
69418.m: Since 1750, Lengnau had the first modern synagogue in Switzerland.

69419.q: How did many Jews in Endingen and Lengnau earn their living, since farming and crafts were forbidden to them?
69419.e: The Surbtal Jews traded horses and cattle or travelled the countryside as pedlars. The fairs in Zurzach and the market in Baden were important.
69419.m: The Surbtal Jews lived mainly from trade.

69420.q: What did the Jews in Endingen and Lengnau regularly have to buy at a high price to be allowed to stay?
69420.e: From 1696, the Jews had to buy a new letter of protection every 16 years. Without renewal they faced expulsion.
69420.m: The Surbtal Jews could only live in the country with a purchased letter of protection.

69421.q: What lies between the villages of Endingen and Lengnau?
69421.e: The Jewish cemetery was laid out in 1750, because before that the Jews had to bury their dead on an island in the Rhine. It is still an important testimony to Jewish life in Aargau.
69421.m: An old Jewish cemetery lies between Endingen and Lengnau.

69422.q: Which textiles were found in the 1960s in the women's gallery of the Lengnau synagogue?
69422.e: Torah binders, in Hebrew mappot, are embroidered bands sewn from boys' swaddling cloths and tied around the Torah scroll. The collection is now in the Jewish Museum of Switzerland.
69422.m: A large collection of Torah binders was found in Lengnau.

69423.q: Where did most Jews from Endingen and Lengnau move after they were given equal rights?
69423.e: With freedom of settlement they could trade and run businesses in the growing cities. As a result, Endingen's population fell by almost half.
69423.m: After gaining equal rights, many Surbtal Jews moved to Zurich.

69424.q: According to the 1860 census, roughly how many Jews lived in Switzerland?
69424.e: The 1860 census recorded 4,216 Israelites and other non-Christians, only about 0.2 percent of the population. Only with the constitutional revision of 1866 did they gain freedom of settlement.
69424.m: Around 1860, only about 4,000 Jews lived in Switzerland.

69425.q: In which two Aargau villages were Jews for a long time the only places in Switzerland where they were allowed to live?
69425.e: From the 18th century, Jews in the old Confederation were only allowed to live in the Surbtal villages of Endingen and Lengnau. They only received local citizenship there in 1879.
69425.m: Endingen and Lengnau in the Surbtal were for a long time the only Jewish villages in Switzerland.

69426.q: Which country was the first in Europe to give Jews fully equal legal rights in 1791?
69426.e: In the course of the Revolution, the French National Assembly granted all Jews full civil rights. The example influenced many countries in Europe.
69426.m: In 1791 France was the first country in Europe to give Jews full civil rights.

69427.q: Did Swiss Jews receive citizenship in the Helvetic Republic from 1798?
a: No, they were still regarded as foreigners
Yes, all of them at once and everywhere
Yes, but only in the towns
69427.e: The Helvetic Republic did abolish torture and feudal burdens, but the opponents of equal rights won. Jews were not declared citizens.
69427.m: The Helvetic Republic also refused Jews citizenship.

69428.q: What happened after the Aargau Grand Council passed a law on equal rights for Jews in 1862?
a: The people forced new elections and the law was repealed
The law came into force at once
The Federal Council declared it invalid
The Jews themselves rejected the law
69428.e: Opponents used a recall initiative to demand the dissolution of parliament. The newly elected Grand Council repealed the emancipation law.
69428.m: In Aargau, equal rights failed in 1862 because of popular resistance.

69429.q: Which state guaranteed civil rights regardless of religion by law in 1869?
69429.e: The law of 3 July 1869 lifted all restrictions based on religion. With the founding of the empire in 1871 it applied throughout the German Empire.
69429.m: In the North German Confederation, Jews gained equal legal rights in 1869.

69430.q: What does it mean when a canton grants a Jewish community recognition under public law?
a: It gets a status similar to the established churches
It becomes the state religion of the canton
It no longer has to obey laws
It may no longer accept members
69430.e: Communities recognised under public law are close to the established churches, for example in the right to levy taxes. In 1972 Basel-Stadt was the first canton to recognise a Jewish community.
69430.m: Recognition under public law puts a community on a similar footing to the established churches.

69431.q: Who was elected to the Federal Council in 1993 as its first member of Jewish origin?
69431.e: The Social Democrat from Geneva comes from an old Surbtal family. In 1999 she also became the first woman President of the Swiss Confederation.
69431.m: Ruth Dreifuss was the first Jewish Federal Councillor.

69432.q: On which issue did the SIG (Swiss Federation of Jewish Communities) mediate between the Swiss authorities and the World Jewish Congress in the 1990s?
69432.e: It was about accounts of Holocaust victims held in Swiss banks that had never been paid out. The debate led to a broad reappraisal of the war years.
69432.m: The SIG mediated on the question of dormant assets.

69433.q: What was the “J stamp” that Switzerland helped demand from Germany in 1938?
a: A mark in the passports of German Jews
An ID card for Jewish soldiers in Switzerland
A postage stamp of the Jewish communities
69433.e: With the “J” in the passport, Swiss border officials could recognise and turn away Jewish refugees. In 1995 the Federal Council apologised for this.
69433.m: The J stamp was meant to make Jewish refugees recognisable at the border.

69434.q: Which ban did the SIG fight against especially in the first decades after it was founded?
69434.e: The ban on ritual slaughter had been in the Federal Constitution since 1893. For a long time the SIG campaigned in vain for it to be lifted.
69434.m: From the start, the SIG fought the ban on kosher slaughter.

69435.q: With which foundation does the SIG publish an annual report on antisemitism for German-speaking Switzerland?
a: Swiss Academies of Arts and Sciences
69435.e: The report records reported antisemitic incidents online and in everyday life. For French-speaking Switzerland, another organisation produces its own report.
69435.m: Every year the SIG and GRA document antisemitic incidents.

69436.q: What is the second Jewish umbrella organisation in Switzerland called, in which liberal communities have joined together?
a: Platform of Liberal Jews of Switzerland
Union of Progressive Communities of Helvetia
69436.e: The PLJS represents liberal communities, for example in Zurich and Geneva. It works closely with the SIG on many issues.
69436.m: Besides the SIG there is the Platform of Liberal Jews of Switzerland.

69437.q: Rolf Bloch, SIG president from 1992 to 2000, ran which Bernese family business?
69437.e: Camille Bloch makes, among other things, Ragusa chocolate. Rolf Bloch led the SIG during the debate on dormant assets.
69437.m: Rolf Bloch was a chocolate maker and president of the SIG.

69438.q: What is the SIG called in French?
69438.e: The French abbreviation is FSCI. The federation represents communities in all language regions.
69438.m: In French, the SIG is called Fédération suisse des communautés israélites.

69439.q: Who made the term “antisemitism” well known in Germany from 1879?
69439.e: The journalist Wilhelm Marr founded the League of Antisemites in 1879. The new term was meant to present hatred of Jews as a seemingly scientific, racist attitude.
69439.m: Wilhelm Marr spread the word antisemitism.

69440.q: What is the mainly religiously based hostility towards Jews in the Christian Middle Ages called?
69440.e: Anti-Judaism accused Jews, for example, of not recognising Jesus as the Messiah. Modern antisemitism, by contrast, argues in racist terms.
69440.m: Anti-Judaism is religiously based hostility towards Jews.

69441.q: Which false accusation led to persecutions of Jews all over Europe during the great plague of 1348/49?
69441.e: Jews were accused of poisoning the wells and so causing the plague. Thousands were murdered or driven out.
69441.m: During the plague, Jews were falsely accused of poisoning wells.

69442.q: What happened to the Jews in Basel in January 1349?
a: Many were burned on an island in the Rhine
They were admitted to the town council
They were allowed to build a synagogue
69442.e: In the Basel pogrom, the Jews were locked in a wooden house on a sandbank in the Rhine and burned. Survivors were expelled from the city.
69442.m: In the Basel pogrom of 1349, Jews were murdered.

69443.q: Which affair about a wrongly convicted Jewish officer divided France from 1894?
69443.e: Captain Alfred Dreyfus was falsely accused of treason. Émile Zola defended him in 1898 with the open letter “J'accuse”, and in 1906 Dreyfus was cleared.
69443.m: The Dreyfus affair revealed antisemitism in France.

69444.q: What did the court in the Bern trial of 1935 find about the “Protocols of the Elders of Zion”?
a: They are a work by Herzl
69444.e: Jewish communities had sued Frontists who were spreading the text. The court described the supposed plans for a Jewish world conspiracy as a forgery and trash literature.
69444.m: The Bern trial exposed the Protocols of the Elders of Zion as a forgery.

69445.q: At the urging of which state did Germany mark the passports of German Jews with a “J” in autumn 1938?
69445.e: Swiss authorities wanted to be able to recognise and turn away Jewish refugees at the border. In 1995 the Federal Council officially apologised for this policy.
69445.m: The J stamp in German passports went back to a demand from Switzerland.

69446.q: On which night in 1938 did synagogues burn in Germany and Austria during the November pogrom?
69446.e: The SA and SS destroyed synagogues, shops and homes; thousands of Jews were sent to concentration camps. The pogrom marks the shift to open persecution.
69446.m: The November pogrom took place on the night of 9 to 10 November 1938.

69447.q: What has the Swiss anti-racism criminal law punished since 1995?
a: Incitement to hatred and denial of genocide
69447.e: The criminal law (Art. 261bis of the Criminal Code) was approved in a popular vote in 1994. It punishes racial discrimination and also covers Holocaust denial.
69447.m: The anti-racism criminal law prohibits racial discrimination.

69448.q: What did the Church prescribe for Jews in the Middle Ages from 1215?
a: Distinctive clothing such as badges or a Jewish hat
69448.e: The Fourth Lateran Council under Pope Innocent III demanded that Jews be distinguished from Christians by their clothing. In many places they had to wear badges or a pointed hat.
69448.m: From 1215, Jews in many places had to wear marked clothing.

69449.q: What does the Hebrew word “Shoah” mean?
69449.e: Shoah means roughly catastrophe or great disaster. Many Jews prefer the word to the Greek term “Holocaust” (burnt offering).
69449.m: Shoah is the Hebrew word for the catastrophe of the genocide of the Jews.

69450.q: On which day is International Holocaust Remembrance Day?
69450.e: On 27 January 1945, the Red Army liberated the Auschwitz-Birkenau camp. In 2005 the UN declared this day an international day of remembrance.
69450.m: On 27 January the world remembers the victims of the Holocaust.

69451.q: Which title of honour does the Yad Vashem memorial give to non-Jews who saved Jews at the risk of their lives?
69451.e: Yad Vashem in Jerusalem honours rescuers with this title. Several Swiss men and women have also been honoured in this way.
69451.m: Rescuers of Jews are honoured as Righteous Among the Nations.

69452.q: Which St Gallen police commander let hundreds of Jewish refugees enter illegally in 1938 and was only cleared in 1995?
69452.e: He backdated entry visas so that refugees could stay despite the border closure. For this he was dismissed and convicted; a court acquitted him in 1995.
69452.m: Paul Grüninger saved refugees and was only cleared after his death.

69453.q: In which city did the Swiss diplomat Carl Lutz save tens of thousands of Jews with letters of protection in 1944?
69453.e: As vice consul he issued letters of protection and set up protected houses, including the Glass House. It was one of the largest rescue operations of the Second World War.
69453.m: Carl Lutz saved tens of thousands of people in Budapest.

69454.q: What is the name of the expert commission that investigated Switzerland's role in the Second World War from 1996 to 2002?
69454.e: The Independent Commission of Experts under Jean-François Bergier examined refugee policy and economic relations. Among other things, its report criticised the turning away of many refugees.
69454.m: The Bergier Commission researched Switzerland in the Second World War.

69455.q: Which artist has been laying Stolpersteine (“stumbling stones”) in memory of Nazi victims since the 1990s?
69455.e: The small brass plates in the pavement give the names and fates of the victims in front of their last home. They now exist in many countries, including Switzerland.

69456.q: In which Swiss city is the Anne Frank Fonds, founded by Otto Frank, based?
69456.e: Otto Frank, the only survivor of the family, moved to Switzerland after the war and founded the fund in 1963. It manages the rights to his daughter's diary.
69456.m: The Anne Frank Fonds is based in Basel.

69457.q: At which conference in January 1942 did Nazi officials coordinate the murder of the European Jews?
69457.e: On 20 January 1942, senior officials discussed the organisation of the deportations and murders in a villa on Berlin's Wannsee. In total about six million Jews were murdered.
69457.m: The Wannsee Conference organised the genocide of the Jews.

69458.q: Which architect designed the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe in Berlin, opened in 2005?
69458.e: The field of stelae consists of 2,711 concrete blocks of different heights. Beneath it is an information centre with biographies of victims.
69458.m: Peter Eisenman created the Holocaust memorial in Berlin.

69459.q: On which day was the State of Israel proclaimed?
69459.e: On the day before the British Mandate ended, the Declaration of Independence was read out in Tel Aviv. The next day, neighbouring Arab states attacked.

69460.q: Who read out Israel's Declaration of Independence in 1948 and became its first Prime Minister?
69460.e: Ben-Gurion was chairman of the Jewish Agency and led the country as its first head of government. Another Zionist leader became the first President.
69460.m: David Ben-Gurion was Israel's first Prime Minister.

69461.q: What did the UN General Assembly decide about Palestine in 1947?
a: Partition into a Jewish and an Arab state
The founding of a single shared state
69461.e: The partition plan (Resolution 181) provided for two states and an international status for Jerusalem. The Jewish side agreed, the Arab side rejected it.
69461.m: In 1947 the UN decided to partition Palestine.

69462.q: In which document of 1917 did Great Britain support a “national home” for the Jewish people in Palestine?
69462.e: Foreign Secretary Arthur Balfour wrote the letter to Lord Rothschild. At the same time, the rights of the non-Jewish population were to be protected.
69462.m: In 1917 the Balfour Declaration promised a Jewish national home.

69463.q: How many seats does the Knesset, Israel's parliament, have?
69463.e: The 120 members are elected by pure proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency. The number goes back to the “Great Assembly” of ancient times.

69464.q: What is Israel's national anthem called?
69464.e: Hatikvah means “The Hope”. The song expresses the longing for a free people in its own land.
69464.m: Israel's anthem is called Hatikvah, the hope.

69465.q: Who is regarded as the most important reviver of Hebrew as an everyday spoken language?
69465.e: He consistently spoke Hebrew with his family and created a large dictionary with new words. Today Modern Hebrew is an official language of Israel.
69465.m: Eliezer Ben-Yehuda made Hebrew an everyday language again.

69466.q: Which law of 1950 gives Jews from all over the world the right to immigrate to Israel?
69466.e: The law grants every Jew the right to immigrate and to citizenship. It also applies to children and grandchildren of Jews.
69466.m: The Law of Return governs the immigration of Jews to Israel.

69467.q: Who became the first President of Israel in 1949?
69467.e: The chemist had helped bring about the Balfour Declaration as a Zionist leader. In Israel the office of President is mainly ceremonial.
69467.m: Chaim Weizmann was the first President of Israel.

69468.q: What is the ark in the synagogue called in which the Torah scrolls are kept?
69468.e: The Torah ark usually stands against the wall that faces Jerusalem. An embroidered curtain often hangs in front of it.
69468.m: The Torah scrolls are kept in the Aron ha-Kodesh.

69469.q: What is the bimah in a synagogue used for?
a: as a raised platform for reading the Torah
as a pool for the ritual bath
as a place for the choir
69469.e: The Torah scroll is spread out on the bimah and read from. In many synagogues it stands in the middle of the room.
69469.m: The Torah is read from the bimah.

69470.q: What is the light called that burns constantly in front of the Torah ark in a synagogue?
69470.e: Ner Tamid means “eternal light”. It recalls the constantly burning light in the Temple in Jerusalem.
69470.m: The eternal light in the synagogue is called Ner Tamid.

69471.q: In which direction are synagogues traditionally oriented?
69471.e: Worshippers turn towards the site of the former Temple. In Europe, the wall with the Torah ark therefore usually faces east or south-east.

69472.q: Under traditional law, how many people of religious age are needed for a minyan for communal prayer?
69472.e: A minyan consists of ten Jews of religious age, in Orthodox communities only men. Only then may certain prayers be said.

69473.q: Which architectural style shaped many synagogues in the 19th century, for example the New Synagogue in Berlin of 1866?
69473.e: Oriental-looking forms such as horseshoe arches and domes were meant to recall the origins of Judaism and Moorish Spain. This made synagogues clearly different from churches.
69473.m: Many 19th-century synagogues were built in the Moorish style.

69474.q: In which city is the Old New Synagogue, the oldest synagogue in Europe still in use?
69474.e: The Old New Synagogue was built in the 13th century in the Gothic style. Services have been held there almost without interruption ever since.
69474.m: Prague's Old New Synagogue is the oldest synagogue in Europe still in use.

69475.q: Which architect, who later designed the main building of ETH Zurich, built the synagogue in Dresden in 1840?
69475.e: Semper combined Romanesque and oriental forms. The synagogue was destroyed in the November pogrom; in 2001 a new building was put up on the site.
69475.m: Gottfried Semper designed the old Dresden synagogue.

69476.q: Which synagogue is regarded as the largest in Europe?
69476.e: The synagogue in the Hungarian capital was consecrated in 1859 and has about 3,000 seats. It is built in the Moorish style.
69476.m: The Dohány Street Synagogue is the largest synagogue in Europe.

69477.q: What is the philosophical school called for which Martin Buber is particularly known?
69477.e: For Buber, a person only becomes fully human in the encounter with another. For him, real living is encounter.
69477.m: Buber is regarded as a representative of the philosophy of dialogue.

69478.q: Which Jewish devotional movement from Eastern Europe did Martin Buber make known in the West?
69478.e: Buber got to know Hasidism in Galicia. With his retellings of Hasidic tales he made it known to a wide audience.
69478.m: Buber made Hasidism known in the West.

69479.q: Which movement shaped by Theodor Herzl did Martin Buber join as a young man?
69479.e: Buber was already working for the Zionist movement around 1900. However, he stood for a more cultural Zionism than Herzl.
69479.m: Buber was a culturally minded Zionist.

69480.q: Why did Martin Buber have to give up teaching in Germany in 1933?
a: Because he was called to America
69480.e: After 1933, Jews were no longer allowed to teach at German universities. Buber emigrated to Jerusalem in 1938.
69480.m: Buber lost his teaching post in 1933 because of the Nazis.

69481.q: What does Martin Buber mean by an I-Thou relationship?
a: A real, whole encounter with another
A business deal between two partners
69481.e: In the I-Thou relationship, a person meets the other directly and without any purpose. If he merely uses the other, Buber speaks of I-It.
69481.m: For Buber, I-Thou is real encounter.

69482.q: Which basic word does Buber set against the relationship “I-Thou”?
69482.e: In I-It, a person experiences the world as an object to use or describe. In I-Thou, he meets another fully and directly.
69482.m: Buber distinguishes the basic words I-Thou and I-It.

69483.q: Who called and chaired the First Zionist Congress?
69483.e: The Viennese journalist and writer invited representatives of Jewish communities from many countries. The congress elected him president of the new movement.
69483.m: Theodor Herzl organised the First Zionist Congress.

69484.q: Roughly how many delegates took part in the First Zionist Congress?
69484.e: 204 delegates came from Jewish communities in many countries. In addition there were guests and journalists.
69484.m: About 200 delegates took part in the First Zionist Congress.

69485.q: Which organisation was founded at the First Zionist Congress?
69485.e: The Zionist Organization was to put the aims of the Basel Programme into practice. Other Zionist institutions were only set up in later years.
69485.m: The World Zionist Organization was founded in Basel in 1897.

69486.q: Which 1896 work by Theodor Herzl laid the intellectual groundwork for the First Zionist Congress?
69486.e: In it, Herzl called for a state of their own as an answer to antisemitism. The work made him famous overnight.
69486.m: Herzl's “The Jewish State” was published in 1896.

69488.q: Which aim did the First Zionist Congress set out in the Basel Programme?
a: A home for the Jewish people in Palestine
Equal rights for Jews in Switzerland
The founding of a Jewish world bank
The return of the Jews to Spain
69488.e: The Basel Programme called for a home in Palestine secured under public law. It became the foundation of the Zionist movement.
69488.m: The Basel Programme called for a Jewish home in Palestine.

69489.q: Which anniversary of the First Zionist Congress was marked by a jubilee congress in Basel in August 2022?
69489.e: 125 years passed between 1897 and 2022. Because of the security situation, the jubilee took place under heavy police protection.
69489.m: In 2022 Basel celebrated the 125th anniversary of the First Zionist Congress.

69490.q: Which country has the most Muslims in the world?
69490.e: More than 230 million Muslims live in Indonesia. Even so, Islam is not the state religion there: the state officially recognises six religions.
69490.m: Indonesia is the country with the most Muslims.

69491.q: What role do Muslim mass organisations such as Nahdlatul Ulama play in Indonesia?
a: They run schools, hospitals and social services
They are state authorities that control mosques
They are trading companies for halal products
They make up the country’s army
69491.e: Nahdlatul Ulama was founded in 1926 on Java and has tens of millions of members. It runs countless schools and social institutions.
69491.m: Nahdlatul Ulama is Indonesia’s largest Muslim organisation.

69492.q: What did the reform movement Muhammadiyah, founded in Indonesia in 1912, want?
a: To purify Islam of added local customs and modernise it
To make Hinduism the state religion
To place Indonesia under Ottoman rule
69492.e: Ahmad Dahlan founded Muhammadiyah in Yogyakarta. The movement focuses on modern education and still runs thousands of schools and universities today.
69492.m: Muhammadiyah is a modernist reform movement in Indonesia.

69493.q: Is Islam the state religion in Indonesia?
a: No, the state recognises several religions
69493.e: The state philosophy Pancasila requires belief in one God but does not favour any particular religion. Six religions are recognised.
69493.m: Indonesia has many Muslims but no state religion.

69494.q: Which Indonesian province is the only one to apply Sharia in criminal law too?
69494.e: Aceh in northern Sumatra received special autonomy after the 2005 peace agreement. Islamic criminal laws apply there, for example with public caning.
69494.m: Aceh is the only province in Indonesia with Sharia criminal law.

69495.q: Which religion did Friedrich Silaban, the architect of the Istiqlal Mosque in Jakarta, belong to?
69495.e: The Protestant Batak Friedrich Silaban won the architecture competition for the national mosque. The Istiqlal Mosque, opened in 1978, is seen as a symbol of religious tolerance.
69495.m: Indonesia’s national mosque was designed by a Christian architect.

69496.q: What is a pesantren in Indonesia?
69496.e: In the pesantren, pupils live with a teacher, the kyai, and learn the Quran, Arabic and Islamic law. Many now also offer state school subjects.
69496.m: Pesantren are Indonesia’s Islamic boarding schools.

69497.q: What did Abdurrahman Wahid, President of Indonesia from 1999 to 2001, particularly stand up for?
69497.e: Abdurrahman Wahid, known as Gus Dur, was for a long time chairman of Nahdlatul Ulama. He was regarded as a champion of pluralism and tolerance.
69497.m: Abdurrahman Wahid was a Muslim scholar and President of Indonesia.

69498.q: What does the concept of “Islam Nusantara” mean in Indonesia?
a: An Islam that respects local culture and traditions
An Islam only for the capital
69498.e: Nusantara is an old name for the Indonesian archipelago. The concept stresses that Islam does not have to push out local traditions.
69498.m: Islam Nusantara stands for a culturally rooted Islam in Indonesia.

69499.q: Which institution in Cairo is regarded as the most important teaching authority of Sunni Islam?
69499.e: Al-Azhar was founded in the 10th century under the Fatimids. Its Grand Imam is today seen as one of the most influential voices of Sunni Islam.
69499.m: Al-Azhar in Cairo is the best-known Sunni university.

69500.q: In which city is Al-Qarawiyyin, founded in 859 by Fatima al-Fihri?
69500.e: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez (Morocco) began as a mosque with teaching. It is regarded as the oldest existing educational institution in the world.
69500.m: Al-Qarawiyyin in Fez was founded by a woman.

69501.q: Which branch of Islam, with large brotherhoods such as the Muridiyya, shapes religious life in Senegal?
69501.e: In Senegal most Muslims belong to a Sufi brotherhood. The Muridiyya was founded by Amadou Bamba and stresses work as worship.
69501.m: In Senegal, Islam is strongly shaped by Sufi brotherhoods.

69502.q: What is the Senegalese city of Touba known for?
a: As a holy city and the destination of a large pilgrimage
As the largest port in West Africa
As the seat of the African Union
69502.e: At the Grand Magal, millions of people come to Touba every year. They remember Amadou Bamba’s exile by the French in 1895.
69502.m: Touba is the holy city of the Murids in Senegal.

69503.q: What is a Sufi order such as the Tijaniyya, widespread in Africa?
a: A community of Islamic mystics around a master
69503.e: Sufi orders practise a mystical form of Islam with prayers, chants and a spiritual teacher. The Tijaniyya has millions of followers, above all in Senegal, Nigeria and Morocco.
69503.m: The Tijaniyya is one of the largest Sufi orders in Africa.

69504.q: Which building in Mali is regarded as the largest mud-brick building in the world?
69504.e: Today’s mosque of Djenné was built in 1907 and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At the annual “Crépissage” festival the inhabitants renew the mud plaster together.
69504.m: The Great Mosque of Djenné is built of mud.

69505.q: Which East African Bantu language is strongly influenced by Arabic through Muslim trading culture?
69505.e: Swahili developed on the coast of East Africa through contact with Arab and Persian traders. The name comes from the Arabic word for “coasts”.
69505.m: Swahili is an African language with many Arabic words.

69506.q: Which city in Mali is known for tens of thousands of historic Islamic manuscripts that were saved from Islamists in 2012 and 2013?
69506.e: From the 15th to the 16th century Timbuktu was a centre of Islamic scholarship. During the occupation by Islamists, librarians secretly smuggled many manuscripts to Bamako.
69506.m: Timbuktu is famous for its old Islamic manuscripts.

69507.q: Roughly what share of all Muslims worldwide belong to Shia Islam?
69507.e: The vast majority of Muslims are Sunni. Estimates put Shias at 10 to 15 per cent, mainly in Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, India and Azerbaijan.
69507.m: Shias are a minority of about one eighth of Muslims.

69508.q: In which of these countries do Shias form the majority of Muslims?
69508.e: In Azerbaijan an estimated two thirds or so of Muslims are Shia. Other countries with a Shia majority are Iran, Iraq and Bahrain.
69508.m: Azerbaijan is one of the few countries with a Shia majority.

69509.q: What is the largest branch within Shia Islam?
69509.e: The Twelver Shias recognise twelve imams, the last of whom, according to their teaching, lives in hiding and will return. The vast majority of Shias belong to them.

69510.q: Which Iraqi city is the destination of the Arbaeen pilgrimage, one of the largest gatherings of pilgrims in the world?
69510.e: The Arbaeen pilgrimage takes place 40 days after Ashura and commemorates Husayn ibn Ali, who is buried in Karbala. Every year millions of people make the pilgrimage, many on foot.
69510.m: Millions of Shias come to Karbala every year for the Arbaeen pilgrimage.

69511.q: In Shia Islam, what is a high-ranking scholar called whose legal interpretation believers follow?
69511.e: Marja al-Taqlid means “source of emulation”. Believers choose such a grand ayatollah and follow his opinions in religious matters.
69511.m: In matters of faith, Shias follow a Marja al-Taqlid.

69512.q: Which Iraqi city with the shrine of Ali is the most important centre of Shia scholarship in Iraq?
69512.e: Najaf is home to the tomb of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the first imam of the Shias. Its hawza, a traditional seminary, is one of the most important in the Shia world.
69512.m: With the shrine of Ali, Najaf is a centre of Shia theology.

69513.q: Which Shia branch does the Houthi movement in Yemen belong to?
69513.e: The Zaydis recognise Zayd ibn Ali as imam and are close to the Sunnis on many legal questions. Zaydi imams ruled North Yemen until 1962.
69513.m: The Houthis in Yemen come from the Zaydi tradition.

69514.q: Which Sunni school of law has the most followers worldwide?
69514.e: The Hanafi school of law goes back to Abu Hanifa and was the official school of the Ottoman Empire. Today it is widespread above all in Turkey and in Central and South Asia.
69514.m: The Hanafi school is the largest Sunni school of law.

69515.q: Who led the Islamic Revolution of 1979 in Iran?
69515.e: Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini returned from exile in Paris in February 1979 after the Shah had left the country. He became the first Supreme Leader of the Islamic Republic.
69515.m: Ayatollah Khomeini was the leader of the Islamic Revolution.

69516.q: According to the constitution, who holds supreme power in the state in the Islamic Republic of Iran?
69516.e: Under the principle of Velayat-e Faqih (“guardianship of the jurist”), a Shia legal scholar leads the state. The President is below him.
69516.m: In Iran a legal scholar holds power in the state as Supreme Leader.

69517.q: Who became Iran’s Supreme Leader in 1989 after Khomeini’s death?
69517.e: Ali Khamenei had previously been President. In June 1989 he was chosen as Khomeini’s successor as Supreme Leader.

69518.q: Which twelve-member Iranian body checks laws for compatibility with Islam and approves election candidates?
69518.e: The Guardian Council consists of six Islamic jurists and six lawyers. Because it can exclude candidates, it has great influence on elections.
69518.m: In Iran, the Guardian Council decides who may stand for election.

69519.q: According to the Iranian constitution, which body is responsible for choosing the Supreme Leader?
69519.e: The Assembly of Experts consists of about 88 clerics elected by the people. It chooses the Supreme Leader and is also supposed to supervise him.
69519.m: The Assembly of Experts chooses Iran’s Supreme Leader.

69520.q: How was the Islamic Republic of Iran founded in spring 1979?
a: By a decree of the Shah
69520.e: On 30 and 31 March 1979 the population voted for the Islamic Republic in a referendum. It was proclaimed on 1 April 1979.
69520.m: The Islamic Republic of Iran was created in 1979 by a referendum.

69521.q: In which Iranian city is the shrine of the eighth imam, Ali al-Rida (Reza)?
69521.e: The Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad is one of the largest religious complexes in the world. Millions of pilgrims visit it every year.
69521.m: With the Imam Reza shrine, Mashhad is Iran’s largest place of pilgrimage.

69522.q: After the death of which young woman in the custody of the morality police did nationwide protests break out in Iran in 2022?
69522.e: Jina Mahsa Amini had been arrested because her headscarf was allegedly not worn correctly, and she died in September 2022. The protests were held under the slogan “Woman, Life, Freedom”.
69522.m: The death of Jina Mahsa Amini triggered large protests in Iran in 2022.

69523.q: What title has the King of Saudi Arabia officially held since 1986?
a: Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques
69523.e: In 1986 King Fahd replaced the form of address “Majesty” with this title. It emphasises responsibility for the holy sites in Mecca and Medina.
69523.m: The Saudi king calls himself Custodian of the Two Holy Mosques.

69524.q: Which power did the Saudi religious police lose in April 2016?
69524.e: Since 2016 the religious police (the Committee for the Promotion of Virtue and the Prevention of Vice, also called the mutawwa) may no longer pursue or arrest anyone. It must report suspected cases to the regular police.
69524.m: Since 2016 the Saudi religious police may no longer arrest anyone.

69525.q: In which month of the Islamic calendar does the Hajj take place?
69525.e: The name Dhu al-Hijjah means “the one of the pilgrimage”. The main rites take place from the 8th to the 13th day of this month.
69525.m: The Hajj takes place in the twelfth Islamic month.

69526.q: What applies to non-Muslims with regard to the city of Mecca?
a: They may not enter the city.
They may not enter only during Ramadan.
They may enter only with an escort.
69526.e: The holy area of Mecca is reserved for Muslims. On the access roads, signs direct non-Muslims to bypass roads.

69527.q: What is the name of Saudi Arabia’s reform programme, presented in 2016, which aims to make the economy less dependent on oil?
69527.e: Vision 2030 was presented by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. Among other things, it focuses on tourism, entertainment and new industries.
69527.m: With Vision 2030, Saudi Arabia wants to depend less on oil.

69528.q: Who proclaimed the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932?
69528.e: Abdulaziz ibn Saud united the regions of Najd and Hejaz. All later kings were his sons.
69528.m: Abdulaziz ibn Saud founded Saudi Arabia in 1932.

69529.q: Which rite is regarded as the essential high point of the Hajj?
69529.e: On 9 Dhu al-Hijjah the pilgrims stand praying on the plain of Arafat from midday until sunset. Anyone who misses this day has not performed a valid Hajj.
69529.m: Without the day at Mount Arafat the Hajj is not valid.

69530.q: Since which year has Saudi Arabia issued tourist visas to travellers without a religious or business purpose?
69530.e: In September 2019 Saudi Arabia introduced a tourist visa that can also be applied for online. Before that, almost only pilgrims, business people and workers came into the country.
69530.m: Since 2019 tourists have been able to visit Saudi Arabia normally.

69531.q: What is the English name of the Turkish authority Diyanet İşleri Başkanlığı?
69531.e: The authority was founded in 1924 and is responsible for all matters of Sunni Islam in Turkey. It is usually simply called Diyanet for short.
69531.m: The Diyanet is the Turkish Presidency of Religious Affairs.

69532.q: What is one of the tasks of the Turkish religious authority Diyanet?
a: It employs the imams of the mosques.
69532.e: The Diyanet manages tens of thousands of mosques in Turkey. The imams there are state employees and are paid by the state.
69532.m: In Turkey, imams are employees of the Diyanet.

69533.q: In Turkey, who usually writes the texts for the Friday sermon in the mosques?
69533.e: Each week the Diyanet issues a standard sermon that is read out throughout the country. In this way the state influences religious content.
69533.m: In Turkey the Friday sermon is set centrally.

69534.q: Since the introduction of the presidential system in 2018, who has the Diyanet been answerable to?
69534.e: The Diyanet used to come under the Prime Minister. With the presidential system it was attached directly to the office of the President.
69534.m: The Diyanet is answerable to the Turkish President.

69535.q: What is the name of the large mosque association in Germany that is closely linked to the Turkish Diyanet?
69535.e: The Turkish-Islamic Union for Religious Affairs was founded in 1984. It is one of the largest mosque associations in Germany.
69535.m: DITIB is the arm of the Diyanet in Germany.

69536.q: In which city was the large DITIB Central Mosque opened in 2018?
69536.e: The mosque in the Ehrenfeld district was designed by the architect Paul Böhm. Turkish President Erdoğan was present at the opening in September 2018.
69536.m: The DITIB Central Mosque is in Cologne-Ehrenfeld.

69537.q: What does the Diyanet send to countries such as Germany, Austria or Switzerland?
69537.e: The imams are sent abroad for a few years and paid by the Turkish state. Critics therefore call for more imams to be trained in their own country.
69537.m: The Diyanet sends paid imams to Turkish mosques abroad.

69538.q: Which religious community in Turkey prays not in a mosque but in a cemevi, and does not feel represented by the Diyanet?
69538.e: The Alevis particularly revere Ali and have their own rituals such as the cem service. Because the Diyanet follows Sunni Hanafi teaching, they call for recognition of their own.
69538.m: The Alevis hold their worship in a cemevi.

69539.q: What did the German Council of Science and Humanities recommend in 2010?
a: To set up Islamic theology at state universities
To ban the building of mosques
To bring imams only from Turkey
69539.e: The Council advises the federal and state governments on questions concerning universities. Its recommendation led to the founding of several state-funded centres.
69539.m: In 2010 the Council gave the impetus for Islamic theology at German universities.

69540.q: Who, among others, do centres for Islamic theology such as the one in Tübingen train?
69540.e: The centre in Tübingen opened in January 2012 as the first in Germany. Among others, it trains Islamic religious education teachers and theologians.
69540.m: Tübingen had the first centre for Islamic theology in Germany.

69541.q: Which image of God does the Münster theologian Mouhanad Khorchide emphasise?
a: A distant God who never intervenes
69541.e: In 2012 Mouhanad Khorchide published the book “Islam is Mercy”. With it he sparked debates with Islamic associations.
69541.m: Mouhanad Khorchide stands for a theology of mercy.

69542.q: At which Swiss university was the Swiss Centre for Islam and Society (SZIG) founded in 2015?
69542.e: The SZIG at the University of Fribourg offers further education for imams, chaplains and professionals. It links Islamic theology with questions of Swiss society.
69542.m: The Swiss Centre for Islam and Society is in Fribourg.

69543.q: What was disputed when the Institute of Islamic Theology at the Humboldt University in Berlin was founded?
a: The influence of the Islamic associations
Arabic as the language of teaching
69543.e: The institute was founded in 2018 and started teaching in 2019. It was disputed how much say the Islamic associations should have on the advisory board.
69543.m: Since 2019 Berlin has had an Institute of Islamic Theology at the Humboldt University.

69545.e: Fiqh literally means “understanding”. Scholars derive rules from it for prayer, fasting, family and trade.

69546.q: Which subject at Islamic theological faculties studies the reported sayings and deeds of Muhammad?
69546.e: A hadith is a handed-down report about Muhammad. Hadith studies mainly check the chain of transmitters (isnad) for reliability.
69546.m: Hadith studies examine reports about the Prophet.

69547.q: Why did Germany ban the Islamic Centre Hamburg in 2024?
a: It was regarded as an outpost of the Iranian leadership
It was in a nature reserve
69547.e: With the ban, the Shia Imam Ali Mosque on the Alster was also closed. Because of its tiles it is also called the “Blue Mosque”.
69547.m: The Imam Ali Mosque in Hamburg was closed in 2024.

69548.q: In which city was one of the largest mosques in Western Europe opened in 1995?
69548.e: The Great Mosque of Rome is on Monte Antenne. The architect Paolo Portoghesi combined Islamic forms with Roman architecture.
69548.m: The Great Mosque of Rome was opened in 1995.

69549.q: Money from which country mainly funded the Great Mosque of Geneva, opened in 1978?
69549.e: The mosque in the Petit-Saconnex district was funded by the Muslim World League, based in Mecca. Its minaret is 22 metres high.
69549.m: The Great Mosque of Geneva was built with Saudi money.

69550.q: Which mosque was opened in 1926 in gratitude to the Muslim soldiers who had fought for France in the First World War?
69550.e: The Great Mosque of Paris was built in the Moorish style. The French state helped fund it, even though it is strictly secular.
69550.m: The Great Mosque of Paris commemorates Muslim soldiers of the First World War.

69551.q: When was the first purpose-built mosque in Great Britain opened?
69551.e: The Shah Jahan Mosque in Woking was built by the orientalist Gottlieb Wilhelm Leitner. At that time Britain ruled India with its many Muslims.
69551.m: Great Britain’s first purpose-built mosque is in Woking.

69553.q: What was the Fazl Mosque in London, opened in 1926, long known for?
a: As the seat of the head of the Ahmadiyya
As the largest mosque in Europe
As a mosque only for women
As a museum of Islamic art
69553.e: The Fazl Mosque in the Southfields district is regarded as London’s first purpose-built mosque. For a long time it was the seat of the head of the Ahmadiyya community.
69553.m: The Fazl Mosque is London’s oldest purpose-built mosque.

69554.q: In which canton is Wangen bei Olten, whose minaret dispute helped trigger the minaret initiative?
69554.e: In 2005 a Turkish cultural association wanted to build a minaret on its clubhouse in Wangen bei Olten. The legal dispute, which lasted years, made the issue known throughout Switzerland.
69554.m: The Wangen bei Olten minaret dispute took place in the canton of Solothurn.

69555.q: What do many Muslims celebrate at the festival of Mawlid al-Nabi?
a: The birthday of the Prophet Muhammad
The return of the pilgrims from Mecca
69555.e: Many Sunnis celebrate the Mawlid on 12 Rabi al-Awwal with poems, prayers and festivities. Some strict movements reject the festival as a later innovation.
69555.m: Mawlid al-Nabi is the Prophet’s birthday.

69556.q: Which month does the Islamic year begin with?
69556.e: Muharram is the first month of the Islamic lunar year. New Year is usually marked more quietly than the two major festivals.
69556.m: The Islamic year begins with the month of Muharram.

69557.q: Which year of the Islamic lunar calendar began in June 2026?
